full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsLEH must not be overlooked during a dental examination. It can cause problems with esthetics, tooth sensitivity, malocclusion, and an increased risk of dental caries. In its mildest form, LEH is often misdiagnosed as decay, as most teeth are prone to decay. Early recognition of LEH is critical because it primarily concerns aesthetics. Dentists have the chance to prevent these abnormalities through anticipatory guidance. A precise diagnosis is required to differentiate other illnesses and develop a conservative treatment approach if LEH is already present. Early diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis of LEH are crucial for preventing its complications from restoring esthetics and increasing masticatory efficiency.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionLinear enamel hypoplasia (LEH) is identified in populations due to amelogenesis disruption as a sign of stress. Stress in the form of trauma, diet, viral illnesses, and environmental variations can alter enamel matrix production. Stresses in any form leave persistent physical traces on the teeth. Molar incisor hypomineralization (MIH) is a type of enamel defect that is qualitative and caused by decreased mineral density. In contrast, enamel hypoplasia is a quantitative enamel defect resulting from decreased enamel matrix secretion. However, in the most severe cases of MIH, the hypomineralized enamel might fracture, resulting in tissue thickness loss following tooth eruption. Enamel hypoplasia is characterized by a loss in enamel thickness that occurs before tooth eruption and, if associated with a systemic insult, affects all teeth growing at the time. At the transition to normal enamel, hypoplastic enamel lesions have regular margins but tend to fracture under occlusal forces, which are unevenly rough and appear in chalky-white or brownish-discolored areas [1]. Enamel hypoplasia occurs when enamel development is disrupted. The teeth most typically implicated are the central incisors, lateral incisors, canines, and molars; enamel production occurs within the first year following birth [2]. Case presentationA 16-year-old female reported to our department for a routine dental checkup. She did not have any harmful habits from chewing or smoking tobacco. Her past medical history was non-contributory. She had no history of any drug intake for fever or illness. A general examination revealed her vitals were stable. The intraoral examination showed the presence of a linear furrow-like defect on the labial surface of the maxillary anterior teeth and only the maxillary first molars (Figure 1).Figure 1An intraoral examination showed a linear band-like hypoplastic defect on the middle-third of the enamel crown in the maxillary anterior teeth and on the occlusal surface of the maxillary first molars (blue arrows).On further closer examination, a linear hypoplastic enamel defect was observed on the labial surfaces of the mandibular central, lateral, and incisal surfaces of the mandibular canine and first molars. The mandibular premolars and second molars are spared of any such hypoplastic enamel defects (Figure 2).Figure 2An intraoral examination revealed a furrow-like or band-like defect on the labial surface of the mandibular anterior teeth (blue arrows) and the mandibular first molar (yellow arrows).The differential diagnosis for LEH includes MIH, amelogenesis imperfecta, Blaschko linear enamel defects, and odontoclasia. It is important to note that odontoclasia, a linear form of enamel caries in children that arises along the neonatal line, is not just a clinical condition but a social issue. It is commonly seen among impoverished children, highlighting the need for accessible dental care for all. The hypoplastic enamel defect in amelogenesis imperfecta occurs in all the teeth and occurs among families. Blaschko linear enamel defects run as vertical grooves extending along the middle third of the crown of the maxillary central incisors. They occur as a clinical marker in focal dermal hypoplasia, a genetic skin disease. The clinical significance of this case report lies in its description of a case of LEH resulting from stress induced by nutritional deficiency during the chronological eruption of the teeth between the ages of 9 and 11. Therefore, beyond this time of stress, the sequential erupted maxillary and mandibular premolars were not affected.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to explore the clinical features and potential causes of linear enamel hypoplasia (LEH) in relation to childhood illnesses and nutritional challenges.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a case report involving a 16-year-old female who presented with a linear furrow-like defect on the labial surface of her maxillary anterior teeth, with a focus on the impact of early-life stress and malnutrition.
analysis.methods: The study utilized a clinical examination approach to identify enamel defects, including the measurement of hypoplastic areas and the use of a modified z-score to assess deviations in perikymata spacing.
analysis.main_results: The case report identified a linear furrow-like defect on the labial surface of the maxillary anterior teeth, with evidence suggesting that the defect may be linked to physiological stress during the weaning stage and a high-risk diet containing contaminated marine food.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the presence of LEH as an indicator of early-life stress and malnutrition, highlighting its potential role in identifying vulnerable populations for targeted interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that LEH can serve as a valuable marker for assessing early-life nutritional and health challenges, which may inform public health strategies for food supplementation and disease prevention in at-risk groups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single case report, which may not be representative of broader populations. The evidence is based on clinical observations and is considered moderate in strength.

analysis.summary_en: This case report investigates linear enamel hypoplasia (LEH) in a 16-year-old female, linking the defect to early-life physiological stress and malnutrition. The study highlights the potential of LEH as a marker for identifying individuals who experienced nutritional or health challenges during childhood. While the findings suggest a correlation between LEH and early-life stress, the study's reliance on a single case limits its generalizability. The results may inform public health strategies for targeted interventions in at-risk populations, particularly those with a history of malnutrition or dietary exposure to contaminants. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of controlled comparisons.

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将 LEH 的存在解释为生命早期压力和营养不良的一个指标,强调了其在识别弱势群体以采取有针对性的干预措施方面的潜在作用。

elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于单个 病例报告,可能无法代表更广泛的人群。该证据基于临床观察,强度中等。

news.content_title: Measles cases now double last year's total as health experts urge vaccination
news.content: Measles cases now double last year's total as health experts urge vaccination Dr. Todd Ellerin from South Shore Health says speed of surge is not surprising Measles cases now double last year's total as health experts urge vaccination Dr. Todd Ellerin from South Shore Health says speed of surge is not surprising The number of measles infections in the United States is now 4,588. That's more than double last year's total of 2,289 --- and it's only October. For South Shore Health’s Dr. Todd Ellerin, the speed of the surge is not surprising since measles is considered the most contagious virus in the world. He says even small gaps in vaccination coverage can allow outbreaks to spread quickly, particularly in under-vaccinated communities. Why doctors are concerned Ellerin says the country has an effective tool to prevent measles, but vaccination rates remain a concern. “We have the right vaccine,” Ellerin said. “We have a measles problem because people are, you know, not accepting that vaccine.” He also pointed to what he called “epidemics of mistrust” and misinformation as challenges for public health officials. “In 2026, measles should be in our history books, not our hospitals," Ellerin said. What public health officials need to do Ellerin said rebuilding public trust will require more than providing information. He said the CDC should strengthen its public health workforce, improve coordination with state and local health departments and focus on clear, concise communication. He also criticized continued links between the MMR vaccine and autism, saying that connection has been disproven in multiple studies. With cases continuing to rise, he says vaccination and stronger public health communication remain key tools for preventing further spread

analysis.brief_en: As of October 2026, the United States has reported 4,588 measles infections, more than double the 2,289 cases from the previous year. This surge is attributed to gaps in vaccination coverage and the spread of misinformation, particularly regarding the MMR vaccine. Dr. Todd Ellerin from South Shore Health emphasized that measles remains a significant public health concern due to low vaccination rates and 'epidemics of mistrust.' Meeting Coverage > IDWeek Infants' Maternal Measles Protection May Not Last Until First MMR Dose — But moving up the initial dose could come with its own trade-offs by Terrence Rudd, Staff Writer, MedPage Today October 23, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday WASHINGTON -- At 6 months of age, most U.S. infants no longer had detectable levels of maternal neutralizing antibodies for measles, potentially leaving them at risk of an infection months before their first dose of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine at 12 months of age, according to a retrospective analysis. At birth, infants' median concentrations of neutralizing antibodies for three major circulating measles strains exceeded their mothers' levels. But those infant levels began consistently dropping below their moms' levels by 2 months of age. By 6 months, the infants' median neutralizing antibodies had fallen below 120 mIU/mL -- the study's correlate of measles protection -- for all three measles strains. At 6 months, the proportions of infants who were seropositive for the three measles strains were 8.7% for the Edmonston strain (A), 19.6% for Maryland.USA/18.18 (B3), and 17.4% for Missouri.USA/15.18 (D8), reported Buddy Creech, MD, MPH, of Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee. "What this means is that infants are going to be susceptible to measles virus infection sooner than maybe we previously thought," Creech said at the IDWeek annual meeting. "As measles circulation increases, infants are going to be an important vulnerable population to consider in our response." The findings could force a rethink about measles vaccination timing, he cautioned. "The immunologic impact of earlier vaccination, such as 9 or 10 months of age, should be evaluated in a well-powered clinical study," Creech noted. "At the very least, we're going to have to think about what it means to vaccinate in early toddler time -- 12 to 15 months -- and maybe accelerate the second dose." The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends two doses of either the MMR vaccine or the combination MMR and varicella vaccine, with the first dose at age 12-15 months and the second dose at 4-6 years. CDC recommendations mirror those of AAP, though the agency controversially moved to recommend separate MMR and varicella vaccines for the first dose. Further complicating things, the Trump administration has proposed separating all components of the MMR vaccine into individual shots, and spacing them out whenever possible. The findings come as the U.S. grapples with its worst measles case total since 1991. As of Oct. 22, the CDC reported 4,588 cases, already doubling last year's total of 2,289. Nearly all (96%) of this year's cases have happened in people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. While the CDC reports three measles deaths this year, Pennsylvania alone has reported five measles-associated deaths. Despite the spike, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other Trump administration officials continue to fuel vaccine skepticism with disproven claims of vaccine-driven dangers, including from the MMR vaccine. Starting Sooner Comes With Costs Given the range of risks for infants, including subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, why not move up the first measles vaccine dose to 6 months? That's already happening when an infant is going to travel internationally or when they might be exposed to a local outbreak cluster, Creech noted. Measles vaccine effectiveness is very different, however, when the first dose is at 6 months rather than 9 months: 51% versus 83%, according to a 2019 meta-analysis, he cautioned. Vaccinating infants with a first dose at age 9 months might be warranted given higher measles virus circulation in the U.S., he noted, particularly if the U.S. loses its measles elimination status. "I think our data would imply that if we continue to wait until 12-15 months to vaccinate, we're going to have a subsection of our population at risk for measles and for its complications," Creech said. Creech's team analyzed measles binding and neutralizing antibodies in serum samples from maternal-infant pairs and adults in the MOMI-Vax and the Mix & Match studies, which explored COVID-19 vaccination. Most of the infants' 6-month neutralizing-antibody levels were at assays' lower detection limits, a finding that indicates their antibody titers were probably much lower than that, Creech noted. The same downward trend seen in neutralizing antibodies happened with the infants' binding antibody levels. By age 6 months, median levels were below the correlate protection levels. A secondary analysis showed that the immunologic protection given by moms to babies has waned over time as vaccination rates have risen. Among mothers who were born before the 1967 launch of the U.S. measles eradication program, infants' antibody levels remained high enough to likely confer protection for an estimated 6 months. Among mothers born after 1967 -- who didn't face measles infection or residual circulating measles -- infant protection fell to an estimated 4 months. news.title_zh: 婴儿的母体 麻疹 保护可能不会持续到第一次 MMR 剂量
news.source_body_en: A study presented at the IDWeek annual meeting in 2026 found that by 6 months of age, most U.S. infants no longer have detectable levels of maternal neutralizing antibodies for measles, potentially leaving them vulnerable before their first MMR vaccine dose at 12 months. Buddy Creech, MD, MPH, of Vanderbilt University, noted that infants' antibody levels dropped below the correlate of protection by this age. The CDC reported 4,588 measles cases in the U.S. as of October 22, 2026, with three national deaths and five in Pennsylvania. The study highlights the need to reconsider vaccination timing, especially with rising measles circulation, but warns that earlier vaccination may have lower effectiveness. The American Academy of Pediatrics and CDC recommend the first dose at 12-15 months, though the Trump administration has proposed separating MMR vaccine components. These findings may influence future vaccination strategies to protect infants from measles and its complications.

news.title: At the center of the state’s growing measles outbreak, it’s business as usual - Inquirer.com
news.rss_summary_html: At the center of the state’s growing measles outbreak, it’s business as usual  Inquirer.com
news.excerpt_original: At the center of the state’s growing measles outbreak, it’s business as usual Inquirer.com
news.priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
news.content_title: The Philadelphia Inquirer, LLC
news.content: The floats had been decorated, the public officials assembled, and now the parade was underway — a convoy of colorful trailers and pickup trucks rolling slowly through downtown. Firetrucks passed grandmothers in lawn chairs and young children, squealing with delight as they fetched candy tossed by the fistful from passing floats. It was Goose Day in Mifflin County — honoring an animal believed to bring good fortune and prosperity in the coming year — and everywhere you looked were geese: ceramic geese standing sentry on street corners, inflatable geese atop parade floats, goose meat soup over at the Square Cafe, $6.29 a cup. But the day’s joyous tone belied a grim reality. In the midst of the state’s deadliest measles outbreak in decades, Mifflin County — this rural enclave of 46,000 tucked into the rolling hills of the central Pennsylvania valley — had recently achieved a troubling distinction: It now counts the highest rate of infection of any county in the state. For weeks, the nation’s rapid spread of measles — once deemed eradicated in the U.S. thanks to the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine — had been met with growing national alarm. Public health experts issued increasingly sober warnings. News outlets across the country published the latest case totals and measles-related deaths, in a kind of macabre box score. Less than a mile and a half from where paradegoers gathered stood Geisinger Lewistown Hospital, where an 18-year-old Amish girl had been reportedly treated for the measles before ultimately succumbing to a rare complication of the infection last month. She was the state’s fourth measles-related death. A fifth and sixth, in Lancaster and Franklin Counties, soon followed. Yet during a visit to Mifflin County earlier this month, and in conversations with area members of the Amish and non-Amish communities, there were few tangible signs of concern. No widespread panic. No state-held news conferences, like the one organized this summer in Lancaster County, to extoll the benefits of vaccination. At the epicenter of the state’s outbreak, measles seems to have been largely met with a sort of shrugging detachment. By locals outside of the Amish community, who largely see the outbreak as not their problem. By elected officials, who have been reluctant to address publicly the community’s growing public health crisis. Even by members of the Amish community themselves, who — hit disproportionately hard due to low rates of vaccination — have insisted that the virus is simply part of life. As cases here continue a troubling rise, there seems to be, for many, little sense in fretting. “My dad used to say, ‘Worry is from the devil,’” says Mose Yoder, a member of the local Amish community. “We still have to do what we have to do.” Mifflin County is home to an estimated 5,500 Amish people, a community long leery of modern advances, at times including healthcare and vaccines. Mifflin County’s Amish communities tend to be more conservative and traditional than those living in Lancaster County, which has the highest total case counts in the state. The county as a whole trends heavily Republican, a faction in which vaccine skepticism is higher . Seventh-grade measles vaccination rates in the county — which include both Amish and non-Amish students — sit at around 77%, among the lowest in the state. (Philadelphia County, by contrast, is at 97%.) It remains unclear whether — and how far — the outbreak has extended beyond the Amish community to the county’s other residents. But the outbreak has clearly spread widely among the area’s Amish. Vaccination efforts in Mifflin are likely complicated by the local Amish communities’ attitudes around technologies and interaction with outsiders, said Steven Nolt, professor of history and Anabaptist studies and director of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College. “You can’t just say, ‘It’s the law of the land,’” says Helge Hartung, a physician at the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Belleville, which treats a large number of Mifflin County Amish and has been working to vaccinate them. “That doesn’t work.” Since July, 193 cases have been confirmed in Mifflin County, with 76 new cases reported in the last two weeks — more new cases than any county in the state over that period. Both numbers, experts say, are almost certainly significant undercounts. Yet, during a visit to Mifflin County earlier this month, it seemed to largely be business as usual. At the Sharp Shopper grocery store in Belleville, both horse-drawn buggies and late-model SUVs still fill the parking lot. At the Wednesday livestock auction and farmers market, a heavily attended weekly event, men in straw hats and suspenders commingle with guys in pickup trucks and novelty T-shirts (“My wife says I only have two faults: Don’t listen and something else.”). In the small shops and restaurants of downtown Lewistown, patrons talk about the weather and the Eagles’ offense — but not the virus spreading rapidly through their county. “I haven’t heard one customer talk about it,” says Deb Guard, who owns the Lemon & Lime craft shop in downtown Lewistown. “Seriously, not one.” “I haven’t heard one customer talk about it. Seriously, not one.” Even the online rumblings that have been known to percolate here — politically infused back-and-forth about vaccine safety and efficacy — rarely spill into public, residents say. Over at radio station WMRF-FM 95.7, just off the town square, morning host Rocco Pallotto routinely wrangles a chatty stable of listeners. “You ask them [whether] they like apple, pumpkin spice, or caramel better — oh, boy ,” he says. But when Pallotto put out a call recently to discuss news of the local measles outbreak, he didn’t receive anything in response. “There’s just nothing there,” he says. Asked about the rising cases, Amanda Haines, a home health aide and mother of two vaccinated sons from Lewistown, shrugged last week as she sipped coffee outside the East End Coffee Co. As she put it: “I’m more worried about my kid [coming home with] lice.” In Belleville, home to many of Mifflin County’s Amish, it’s difficult to find anyone who hasn’t been touched by the current measles outbreak. It reached Bennie Peachey’s family not long ago, leaving two of his five children — the 9- and the 7-year-old — bedridden, covered “head to toe” in rash. The father himself has so far been spared — “unless I have it now,” said Peachey, a lithe man of 33, as he fussed with a tractor outside the family’s barn. If so, he noted, “It’s not too bad.” The Amish have looked out for each other. They know which neighboring farmhouses are grappling with the infection. They trade home remedies for mitigating the virus’ effects — blackberry juice and yarrow tea for hydration, sunglasses for a sensitivity to light. Some make a point not to bathe while ill, out of an unfounded fear it might push the virus deeper into the body. “We want to take care,” said one Amish woman who declined to give her name. “But we feel that God is in control.” A lack of information — both inside and outside the Amish community — has been an ongoing issue. At least one local Amish newspaper — Die Botschaft — decided not to publish the infection totals and has opted not to wade into coverage of the outbreak, including any recommendations regarding the vaccine. “We just don’t get into that stuff,“ says David Lapp, owner and editor of the Millersburg-based publication. ”It’s not really our focus, or our target.” A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania Department of Health said last week that its efforts to curb the spread of the disease in Mifflin County include distributing “educational materials and ... flyers about vaccine clinics.” The state is working with local healthcare providers to build trust on outreach and vaccination efforts. State Secretary of Health Debra Bogen recently traveled to Mifflin County to meet with local healthcare providers, the spokesperson added, to ensure they “have the tools they need to continue to provide educational information and MMR vaccinations to the affected community.” Local officials, however, have been reluctant to discuss a topic that has routinely devolved into politically infused rhetoric. “We don’t think that we can add much to your inquiry,” Robert Postal, one of three Mifflin County commissioners, said in an email. Some in Mifflin County have filled the void with rumor and innuendo, especially in the weeks following the 18-year-old’s death. The county coroner, a Republican, posted a news release on Facebook saying the young woman died of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a rare and serious neurological complication of measles. Yet the gossip that reached Randy Wilsoncroft, a local who runs a stand at the weekly Belleville auction and market, speculated erroneously the girl suffered from underlying health issues that had exacerbated her infection — even as her father described her, in a September interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, as “perfectly healthy.” “I heard she had West Nile and Lyme disease,” Wilsoncroft said. Back in medical school, when Katie Mascia learned about the measles, the lesson had the feeling of a long-ago relic. “It was almost like a historical lecture — like, ‘Oh, yeah, this is what measles looked like back in our grandparents’ age,’” said Mascia, now director of clinical services at the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Belleville. “I never expected to see a measles case when I graduated from medical school, that’s for sure.” Ever since the first patients began showing up this summer with coughs and fever, she and other local healthcare workers now find themselves on the front lines of responding to an outbreak that has sickened more than 1,200 people statewide. “I never expected to see a measles case when I graduated from medical school, that’s for sure.” Though most people recover from measles without incident, nearly one in five infections reported in Pennsylvania has resulted in hospitalization. In the worst cases, patients arrive struggling to breathe, or must be life-flighted out of Lewistown to larger facilities across the state. Measles-positive mothers in the state have passed the virus on to their newborns, who are sometimes born with rashes and at risk for other severe diseases. Two Lancaster County infants with confirmed cases have died. In the sterile corridors of the county’s clinics and hospitals, patient stoicism can quickly turn to panic. “I see fear,” says Alexander Haines, an inpatient nursing manager at Geisinger Lewistown Hospital, which has treated 72 measles cases to date. “I see a lot of fear.” At the Central Pennsylvania Clinic, physicians have done their best to pierce an often staunch reluctance to a vaccine that has proved 97% effective at preventing the infection. The Amish people who spoke with The Inquirer this month shared a range of opinions that varied widely — sometimes within a single home. Some called the decision not to vaccinate a religious one. Some expressed concern that the side effects of the shots could be greater than the infection itself. Others have received one shot of the MMR vaccine, offering strong protection, but not a second, which experts recommend. “It’s a personal decision,” says Aaron B. Kanagy, a father of eight in Belleville, who contracted the measles as a child, which means he should now have immunity to further illness. Amid the current outbreak, vaccine resistance might be waning. In August and September alone, healthcare providers in Mifflin County administered nearly 800 MMR vaccinations, according to figures provided by the state — a significant jump from the 50 to 75 vaccinations typically administered each month. Last month, meanwhile, the Central Pennsylvania Clinic, which largely treats members of the local Amish and Mennonite communities, held a vaccination clinic locally. Originally, only 15 people signed up to be inoculated. By the time the event was held — just a few days after the death of the 18-year-old on Sept. 11 — 73 people arrived to receive a shot, Mascia said. Still, a wide swath of the area’s Amish — and many other residents — likely remain vulnerable to an airborne disease known to infect nine of 10 unvaccinated people exposed to it. Sitting inside the Belleville clinic, Mascia described the “heartbreak” of the ongoing spread, one that — with cold-and-flu season fast approaching — she fears could pose new challenges, including fewer available hospital beds. As she spoke, the clinic’s executive director appeared in the doorway. “A van with a big 6 on it just pulled in,” the woman reported. Mascia glanced out an office window, watched as an out-of-town TV news truck eased into a parking spot. “We’re very popular lately,” she said. On a vast plot of Belleville land, inside a simple farmhouse, is a small, dark bedroom where the Kanagy family keeps its ill. When the 12-year-old, Lizzie, first contracted the virus last month, the family — Aaron and Katie Kanagy and their eight children — did their best to keep their daughter quarantined even as they braced for a household barrage. By early October, the twins — Lomie and Lena, both 8 years old — hadn’t been feeling well, though they were still on their feet. At the height of the 12-year-old’s illness, Aaron Jr., 7, spent hours at his sister’s bedside, fetching her glasses of water and regaling her with tales from the school day. “I’m pretty much expecting it,” says Katie Kanagy. The Kanagys, like many of the area’s Amish, are old enough to remember the region’s last significant measles outbreak, in the late 1980s, when the infection roiled the Amish community and at least three of the 10 Amish schools across Lawrence and Mercer Counties were temporarily shuttered. But they made it through that OK, they insist. If the infection is coming, Aaron Kanagy said one recent afternoon, as he looked out over the family’s 63 acres of farmland, he would prefer it come soon. “Then,” he said, “it would be done.” While top officials publicly spar over whether Pennsylvanians are dying of measles, a midwife in Amish country believes the outbreak is so bad she wants to be able to carry the MMR vaccine herself. Chester County is the only Philadelphia region county where the virus is actively spreading. Local doctors say they’re worried that even more cases are spreading under the radar in under-vaccinated pockets of Lancaster County, where 31 cases have been detected. The outbreak has spread to more than half of Pennsylvania's 67 counties. Some families are deciding to vaccinate, while others are preparing to get sick. After measles swept through her household, the young woman wanted to get vaccinated. Her doctor said she couldn't because she had leukemia and the treatments had weakened her immune system. At the center of the state’s growing measles outbreak, it’s business as usual

news.content_original: The floats had been decorated, the public officials assembled, and now the parade was underway — a convoy of colorful trailers and pickup trucks rolling slowly through downtown. Firetrucks passed grandmothers in lawn chairs and young children, squealing with delight as they fetched candy tossed by the fistful from passing floats. It was Goose Day in Mifflin County — honoring an animal believed to bring good fortune and prosperity in the coming year — and everywhere you looked were geese: ceramic geese standing sentry on street corners, inflatable geese atop parade floats, goose meat soup over at the Square Cafe, $6.29 a cup. But the day’s joyous tone belied a grim reality. In the midst of the state’s deadliest measles outbreak in decades, Mifflin County — this rural enclave of 46,000 tucked into the rolling hills of the central Pennsylvania valley — had recently achieved a troubling distinction: It now counts the highest rate of infection of any county in the state. For weeks, the nation’s rapid spread of measles — once deemed eradicated in the U.S. thanks to the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine — had been met with growing national alarm. Public health experts issued increasingly sober warnings. News outlets across the country published the latest case totals and measles-related deaths, in a kind of macabre box score. Less than a mile and a half from where paradegoers gathered stood Geisinger Lewistown Hospital, where an 18-year-old Amish girl had been reportedly treated for the measles before ultimately succumbing to a rare complication of the infection last month. She was the state’s fourth measles-related death. A fifth and sixth, in Lancaster and Franklin Counties, soon followed. Yet during a visit to Mifflin County earlier this month, and in conversations with area members of the Amish and non-Amish communities, there were few tangible signs of concern. No widespread panic. No state-held news conferences, like the one organized this summer in Lancaster County, to extoll the benefits of vaccination. At the epicenter of the state’s outbreak, measles seems to have been largely met with a sort of shrugging detachment. By locals outside of the Amish community, who largely see the outbreak as not their problem. By elected officials, who have been reluctant to address publicly the community’s growing public health crisis. Even by members of the Amish community themselves, who — hit disproportionately hard due to low rates of vaccination — have insisted that the virus is simply part of life. As cases here continue a troubling rise, there seems to be, for many, little sense in fretting. “My dad used to say, ‘Worry is from the devil,’” says Mose Yoder, a member of the local Amish community. “We still have to do what we have to do.” Mifflin County is home to an estimated 5,500 Amish people, a community long leery of modern advances, at times including healthcare and vaccines. Mifflin County’s Amish communities tend to be more conservative and traditional than those living in Lancaster County, which has the highest total case counts in the state. The county as a whole trends heavily Republican, a faction in which vaccine skepticism is higher . Seventh-grade measles vaccination rates in the county — which include both Amish and non-Amish students — sit at around 77%, among the lowest in the state. (Philadelphia County, by contrast, is at 97%.) It remains unclear whether — and how far — the outbreak has extended beyond the Amish community to the county’s other residents. But the outbreak has clearly spread widely among the area’s Amish. Vaccination efforts in Mifflin are likely complicated by the local Amish communities’ attitudes around technologies and interaction with outsiders, said Steven Nolt, professor of history and Anabaptist studies and director of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College. “You can’t just say, ‘It’s the law of the land,’” says Helge Hartung, a physician at the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Belleville, which treats a large number of Mifflin County Amish and has been working to vaccinate them. “That doesn’t work.” Since July, 193 cases have been confirmed in Mifflin County, with 76 new cases reported in the last two weeks — more new cases than any county in the state over that period. Both numbers, experts say, are almost certainly significant undercounts. Yet, during a visit to Mifflin County earlier this month, it seemed to largely be business as usual. At the Sharp Shopper grocery store in Belleville, both horse-drawn buggies and late-model SUVs still fill the parking lot. At the Wednesday livestock auction and farmers market, a heavily attended weekly event, men in straw hats and suspenders commingle with guys in pickup trucks and novelty T-shirts (“My wife says I only have two faults: Don’t listen and something else.”). In the small shops and restaurants of downtown Lewistown, patrons talk about the weather and the Eagles’ offense — but not the virus spreading rapidly through their county. “I haven’t heard one customer talk about it,” says Deb Guard, who owns the Lemon & Lime craft shop in downtown Lewistown. “Seriously, not one.” “I haven’t heard one customer talk about it. Seriously, not one.” Even the online rumblings that have been known to percolate here — politically infused back-and-forth about vaccine safety and efficacy — rarely spill into public, residents say. Over at radio station WMRF-FM 95.7, just off the town square, morning host Rocco Pallotto routinely wrangles a chatty stable of listeners. “You ask them [whether] they like apple, pumpkin spice, or caramel better — oh, boy ,” he says. But when Pallotto put out a call recently to discuss news of the local measles outbreak, he didn’t receive anything in response. “There’s just nothing there,” he says. Asked about the rising cases, Amanda Haines, a home health aide and mother of two vaccinated sons from Lewistown, shrugged last week as she sipped coffee outside the East End Coffee Co. As she put it: “I’m more worried about my kid [coming home with] lice.” In Belleville, home to many of Mifflin County’s Amish, it’s difficult to find anyone who hasn’t been touched by the current measles outbreak. It reached Bennie Peachey’s family not long ago, leaving two of his five children — the 9- and the 7-year-old — bedridden, covered “head to toe” in rash. The father himself has so far been spared — “unless I have it now,” said Peachey, a lithe man of 33, as he fussed with a tractor outside the family’s barn. If so, he noted, “It’s not too bad.” The Amish have looked out for each other. They know which neighboring farmhouses are grappling with the infection. They trade home remedies for mitigating the virus’ effects — blackberry juice and yarrow tea for hydration, sunglasses for a sensitivity to light. Some make a point not to bathe while ill, out of an unfounded fear it might push the virus deeper into the body. “We want to take care,” said one Amish woman who declined to give her name. “But we feel that God is in control.” A lack of information — both inside and outside the Amish community — has been an ongoing issue. At least one local Amish newspaper — Die Botschaft — decided not to publish the infection totals and has opted not to wade into coverage of the outbreak, including any recommendations regarding the vaccine. “We just don’t get into that stuff,“ says David Lapp, owner and editor of the Millersburg-based publication. ”It’s not really our focus, or our target.” A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania Department of Health said last week that its efforts to curb the spread of the disease in Mifflin County include distributing “educational materials and ... flyers about vaccine clinics.” The state is working with local healthcare providers to build trust on outreach and vaccination efforts. State Secretary of Health Debra Bogen recently traveled to Mifflin County to meet with local healthcare providers, the spokesperson added, to ensure they “have the tools they need to continue to provide educational information and MMR vaccinations to the affected community.” Local officials, however, have been reluctant to discuss a topic that has routinely devolved into politically infused rhetoric. “We don’t think that we can add much to your inquiry,” Robert Postal, one of three Mifflin County commissioners, said in an email. Some in Mifflin County have filled the void with rumor and innuendo, especially in the weeks following the 18-year-old’s death. The county coroner, a Republican, posted a news release on Facebook saying the young woman died of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a rare and serious neurological complication of measles. Yet the gossip that reached Randy Wilsoncroft, a local who runs a stand at the weekly Belleville auction and market, speculated erroneously the girl suffered from underlying health issues that had exacerbated her infection — even as her father described her, in a September interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, as “perfectly healthy.” “I heard she had West Nile and Lyme disease,” Wilsoncroft said. Back in medical school, when Katie Mascia learned about the measles, the lesson had the feeling of a long-ago relic. “It was almost like a historical lecture — like, ‘Oh, yeah, this is what measles looked like back in our grandparents’ age,’” said Mascia, now director of clinical services at the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Belleville. “I never expected to see a measles case when I graduated from medical school, that’s for sure.” Ever since the first patients began showing up this summer with coughs and fever, she and other local healthcare workers now find themselves on the front lines of responding to an outbreak that has sickened more than 1,200 people statewide. “I never expected to see a measles case when I graduated from medical school, that’s for sure.” Though most people recover from measles without incident, nearly one in five infections reported in Pennsylvania has resulted in hospitalization. In the worst cases, patients arrive struggling to breathe, or must be life-flighted out of Lewistown to larger facilities across the state. Measles-positive mothers in the state have passed the virus on to their newborns, who are sometimes born with rashes and at risk for other severe diseases. Two Lancaster County infants with confirmed cases have died. In the sterile corridors of the county’s clinics and hospitals, patient stoicism can quickly turn to panic. “I see fear,” says Alexander Haines, an inpatient nursing manager at Geisinger Lewistown Hospital, which has treated 72 measles cases to date. “I see a lot of fear.” At the Central Pennsylvania Clinic, physicians have done their best to pierce an often staunch reluctance to a vaccine that has proved 97% effective at preventing the infection. The Amish people who spoke with The Inquirer this month shared a range of opinions that varied widely — sometimes within a single home. Some called the decision not to vaccinate a religious one. Some expressed concern that the side effects of the shots could be greater than the infection itself. Others have received one shot of the MMR vaccine, offering strong protection, but not a second, which experts recommend. “It’s a personal decision,” says Aaron B. Kanagy, a father of eight in Belleville, who contracted the measles as a child, which means he should now have immunity to further illness. Amid the current outbreak, vaccine resistance might be waning. In August and September alone, healthcare providers in Mifflin County administered nearly 800 MMR vaccinations, according to figures provided by the state — a significant jump from the 50 to 75 vaccinations typically administered each month. Last month, meanwhile, the Central Pennsylvania Clinic, which largely treats members of the local Amish and Mennonite communities, held a vaccination clinic locally. Originally, only 15 people signed up to be inoculated. By the time the event was held — just a few days after the death of the 18-year-old on Sept. 11 — 73 people arrived to receive a shot, Mascia said. Still, a wide swath of the area’s Amish — and many other residents — likely remain vulnerable to an airborne disease known to infect nine of 10 unvaccinated people exposed to it. Sitting inside the Belleville clinic, Mascia described the “heartbreak” of the ongoing spread, one that — with cold-and-flu season fast approaching — she fears could pose new challenges, including fewer available hospital beds. As she spoke, the clinic’s executive director appeared in the doorway. “A van with a big 6 on it just pulled in,” the woman reported. Mascia glanced out an office window, watched as an out-of-town TV news truck eased into a parking spot. “We’re very popular lately,” she said. On a vast plot of Belleville land, inside a simple farmhouse, is a small, dark bedroom where the Kanagy family keeps its ill. When the 12-year-old, Lizzie, first contracted the virus last month, the family — Aaron and Katie Kanagy and their eight children — did their best to keep their daughter quarantined even as they braced for a household barrage. By early October, the twins — Lomie and Lena, both 8 years old — hadn’t been feeling well, though they were still on their feet. At the height of the 12-year-old’s illness, Aaron Jr., 7, spent hours at his sister’s bedside, fetching her glasses of water and regaling her with tales from the school day. “I’m pretty much expecting it,” says Katie Kanagy. The Kanagys, like many of the area’s Amish, are old enough to remember the region’s last significant measles outbreak, in the late 1980s, when the infection roiled the Amish community and at least three of the 10 Amish schools across Lawrence and Mercer Counties were temporarily shuttered. But they made it through that OK, they insist. If the infection is coming, Aaron Kanagy said one recent afternoon, as he looked out over the family’s 63 acres of farmland, he would prefer it come soon. “Then,” he said, “it would be done.” While top officials publicly spar over whether Pennsylvanians are dying of measles, a midwife in Amish country believes the outbreak is so bad she wants to be able to carry the MMR vaccine herself. Chester County is the only Philadelphia region county where the virus is actively spreading. Local doctors say they’re worried that even more cases are spreading under the radar in under-vaccinated pockets of Lancaster County, where 31 cases have been detected. The outbreak has spread to more than half of Pennsylvania's 67 counties. Some families are deciding to vaccinate, while others are preparing to get sick. After measles swept through her household, the young woman wanted to get vaccinated. Her doctor said she couldn't because she had leukemia and the treatments had weakened her immune system. news.content_title: Pennsylvania issues alert on congenital measles—something US hasn't seen for decades
news.content: Pennsylvania’s health department issued a health alert Monday as cases of measles in pregnancy and, in turn, cases of congenital measles have continued to increase. Before the current outbreak—which continues to rage across the state—congenital measles cases hadn’t been seen in decades, the department noted in its advisory. The alert included detailed clinical guidance for managing measles exposures and cases during pregnancy as well as cases in newborns. Many doctors have never seen such cases in their careers given the decades of successful use of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But now, with vaccination rates slipping nationwide, the highly infectious virus is better able to get footholds in communities and spread rapidly through under-vaccinated pockets, as is happening in Pennsylvania. As of October 19, Pennsylvania had reported 1,286 measles cases this year across 42 counties. Of those, 247 have been hospitalized, and six people have reportedly died (though the latest reported death is still pending an investigation by the state health department before it is added to the state tally). Ars Video How Scientists Respond to Science Deniers In a response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for Pennsylvania’s health department said officials have confirmed that 66 of the state’s measles cases were in pregnant women. The department does not keep a specific tally of congenital measles cases because the definition of these cases is not currently standardized. However, it noted that that it does track cases by age, and 157 cases have been recorded in children under the age of 4. At least one case of congenital measles led to a death; the first death reported in the current outbreak was in a newborn baby boy , who died immediately after birth while his mother was severely ill with measles. Risky infection Pregnant people who have not been vaccinated against measles nor previously had the infection are susceptible. A case of measles during pregnancy increases the risk of hospitalization, pneumonia, the need for oxygen support or mechanical ventilation, and death. It also increases the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, and preterm labor. The MMR vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy because it is a live attenuated vaccine and poses a theoretical risk of causing an infection in a fetus. If a pregnant person is exposed to the virus, they’re recommended to receive intravenous immunoglobulin to help protect against infection—but only if it is given within six days of exposure. If there’s a measles infection during pregnancy, the measles virus can pass to a fetus in utero or can transmit during or just after birth, leading to a congenital case. These cases can vary widely in symptoms and severity. Some babies will remain asymptomatic while others develop severe, multisystem disease and death. Some common symptoms of congenital measles include fever and jaundice. They can also develop the telltale measles rash, but it is sometimes delayed or atypical given a newborn’s underdeveloped immune system. Other symptoms can include low platelet counts, pneumonia, and neurologic complications. Even if a newborn survives the acute infection, they are at risk of long-term complications. These include immune amnesia, a type of immunosuppression in which the measles virus destroys immune cells and adaptive responses. They are also at risk of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a progressive, fatal neurological disorder that can strike years after an infection. The alert warns that babies with congenital measles need long-term clinical follow-up and monitoring for these neurologic and immunologic complications, and parents need counseling on how to spot early signs of SSPE, which include seizures, regression in milestones, and academic difficulties in older children. This story was updated on October 20 to include case information from the Pennsylvania state health department. Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes. 150 Comments

news.content_title: Wisconsin still fourth-worst in country as measles cases surpass 300
news.content: Wisconsin has surpassed 300 measles cases in 2026 tied to outbreaks in eight counties. The latest data from the Wisconsin Department of Health Services show 308 cases from ongoing outbreaks that began in early July: The largest increase in measles cases reported Oct. 23 comes from Chippewa County, where the count more than doubled since last week. As of Oct. 22, close to 4,600 measles cases have been reported in the U.S., according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . Wisconsin remains the state with the fourth-most cases, behind Pennsylvania, South Carolina and Utah. Experts across the health care field say there's one basic reason to blame: slipping measles vaccination coverage. The country could likely lose its measles elimination status, which was granted in 2000 and means the disease does not circulate continuously. A commission of the World Health Organization is expected to vote on the decision during its meeting in November in Washington, D.C. More: Wisconsin measles cases grow in counties with low vaccination rates More: Measles in Richland County as southwest Wisconsin outbreak keeps growing Measles symptoms typically start a week to two weeks after infection with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A few days after the first symptoms arise, red spots or bumps appear on the face and near the hairline. That rash will spread to the rest of the body. People may also get tiny white spots inside the mouth a few days after symptoms begin. If you think you may have measles, avoid others and call a doctor's office or clinic before showing up to receive medical attention. Wisconsin residents can check their measles, mumps and rubella vaccination status by visiting the Wisconsin Immunization Registry at dhfswir.org . The measles vaccine is covered by most insurance plans and is available at doctors' offices, local health departments, pharmacies and pop-up vaccine clinics.Those who need assistance affording vaccines can access them through the Vaccines for Children and Vaccines for Adults programs. analysis.brief_en: The news report from CIDRAP, published on October 23, 2026, highlights a significant increase in measles cases in the United States, with a total of 4,588 cases reported, more than double the number from the previous year. Pennsylvania is identified as the primary hotspot, contributing nearly 30% of the national cases. The report notes that while the measles vaccine is less effective when given to infants at 6 months, it may still offer protection against severe complications. The situation is described as ongoing, with no specific mention of containment measures or further developments. The data is based on confirmed reports and official tracking, but no details on the source of the outbreak or specific prevention strategies are provided. The report emphasizes the need for continued vigilance and vaccination efforts to control the spread of measles.

Here’s why With five deaths and a sixth under review out of about 1,300 cases, Pennsylvania's measles death rate is running well above historical averages, experts say. Prev Next Pennsylvania's measles outbreak is the largest, deadliest in the US in 30+ years, with 5 deaths among about 1,300 cases and a death rate above average. (Scripps News) By: Deidre McPhillips Posted 5:53 PM, Oct 21, 2026 Share Copy linkFacebookNextdoorXThreadsRedditLinkedInEmailWhatsAppMessengerPrint Add Scripps News as a Google Preferred Source An ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has quickly become the largest and deadliest in the United States in more than 30 years. Historical data suggests that 1 to 3 people will die out of every 1,000 unvaccinated people who contract measles. But Pennsylvania has reported five measles-associated deaths — with a sixth under review — out of about 1,300 total reported cases since the start of the outbreak in April. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE This puts the measles death rate in Pennsylvania at least 1.5 times higher than average — and possibly up to 5 times higher. RELATED STORY | Sixth measles-related death reported as Pennsylvania battles widespread outbreak It’s not likely that the measles virus has changed. One factor might be the size of the outbreak and a probable undercount of cases: It’s difficult to know how many people have been affected. It may also be the unique vulnerabilities of the Pennsylvania community where measles is raging. “There clearly is a shift — not in the biology but a shift in the epidemiology that we’re seeing here in Pennsylvania,” said Dr. Matthew Ferrari, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics at Penn State University. Experts say the outbreak is even larger than official data suggests, and it’s not clear how big it is. The US successfully eliminated measles decades ago, making it difficult to estimate how bad the current resurgence has gotten. A “disease detective” from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention arrived in Pennsylvania this week to help better understand the true scale of the outbreak and its trajectory, the state health department said. The scientist, with the CDC’s Epi-Aid program, is also tasked with evaluating the impact of local vaccination efforts. Scientists and public health workers typically estimate current disease trends by using patterns from recent years, scaling changes against a few variables like birth rates and vaccination rates. But measles data in the US is quite “outdated,” said Dr. Remy Pasco, a research associate at the University of Colorado Boulder. “It’s not endemic, so we don’t have as much data on it. And because the data has been so scarce, anything we can estimate is with a big grain of salt.” IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Measles surge triggers state of emergency in New York Pasco has worked on an analysis to estimate the scale of last year’s measles outbreak in Texas. Some underreporting of cases is expected, he says, but it’s unlikely that the rate of underreporting would be the same — even when comparing recent outbreaks in different parts of the US. There are some “peculiarities” with the outbreak in Pennsylvania, he said. Hospitalization rates with this outbreak are higher than expected. And the Amish and broader Plain community – so named for their simple way of dressing – has a unique way of interacting with the health care system. Severe outcomes, such as hospitalizations and deaths, are generally the best benchmark for understanding how widespread a measles outbreak is, public health experts say. Not every person who is infected with measles will seek care or testing, but severe cases are more visible in the health care system, and tracking them can help set the ratio to understand the full scale. A uniquely susceptible group One signal that this outbreak is different: A disproportionate share of cases are among adults. About two-thirds of measles cases in Pennsylvania have been among adults, and all but a few were unvaccinated. Nationwide, however, cases skew younger; CDC data shows that more than 60% of cases in the US over the past two years have been among children or teens. The large population of unvaccinated adults in Pennsylvania, particularly among Amish and other members of the Plain community, has created a uniquely risky outbreak situation, Ferrari said. Measles complications tend to be more severe for unvaccinated adults than for unvaccinated children, he said. But the low rates of protection among adults in the community also mean vulnerable infants are more likely to be born without protective maternal antibodies. “We normally think about measles as being a childhood infection,” Ferrari said. “Most people have been exposed to measles or have been vaccinated against measles by the time they reach reproductive age.” That’s true around the world. Countries typically have high vaccination rates or endemic measles spread, which means people are exposed when they’re younger. Much of the affected population in Pennsylvania falls into a uniquely susceptible group: both unvaccinated and going decades without exposure because the US had so few cases for so long. If there’s any explanation for a higher death rate than expected in Pennsylvania, Ferrari said, this would be it: Antibodies — whether from vaccination or infection — aren’t being passed on from women of reproductive age to their babies. Two infants who were infected with measles have died in Pennsylvania this year, both too young to receive the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine. “Those are absolutely deaths that wouldn’t have been occurring elsewhere in the world,” Ferrari said. The Pennsylvania Department of Health published an advisory Monday with guidance for measles in pregnancy and congenital measles. “Due to the ongoing measles outbreak, there is an increase in measles cases during pregnancy, along with rising concerns about congenital measles, which has been identified for the first time in decades,” the advisory said. Public health knowledge and guidance on this topic continues to develop, the health department said, but a measles infection increases the risk of complications for pregnant mothers and their babies. ‘Boots on the ground epidemiology’ Another complication to understanding this outbreak is an unusually political fight over measles deaths. Pennsylvania leaders have clashed with federal leaders over measles deaths in Pennsylvania, putting a key data point for understanding the scale of the outbreak into question. Although the state health department has officially reported five measles-associated deaths, the CDC dashboard includes only three — noting that the “number is subject to change” as additional information becomes available and that the agency is working to “develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles.” In September, the Pennsylvania health department “began the formal process of requesting an Epi-Aid” from the CDC, but Dr. Debra Bogen, the department secretary, noted in a letter to CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz that the request would be rescinded “if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths.” Last week, Bogen sent another letter to Schwartz thanking her for the “support and technical assistance from CDC professional staff throughout this outbreak response” and accepting the Epi-Aid as the state health department and CDC staff “continue to collaborate effectively” on measles outbreak response work. “While the Department is prepared to accept this Epi-Aid, I again ask the CDC to acknowledge the loss of five Pennsylvanians to measles and to report these deaths on the CDC’s public dashboard so that we can repair and rebuild trust in the public health system in the U.S.,” Bogen wrote. “By not acknowledging the deaths, the CDC obscures the seriousness of this disease and the toll of measles across the U.S.” Without the historical data to use as a benchmark, understanding the true scale of the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania will require investigative public health work. It’s “classic boots on the ground epidemiology,” Ferrari said, with epidemiologists out and about in the community asking questions about recent health history and vaccination coverage. “These are outbreaks in populations that haven’t seen this in a long time, and so we can’t rely on the standard approaches that are predicated on consistent or persistent transmission.” The-CNN-WireTM & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros. analysis.time: The outbreak began in April 2026, with the latest report on deaths and cases published on October 21, 2026. The death rate is currently at least 1.5 times higher than average.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is occurring in Pennsylvania, USA, primarily affecting the Amish and broader Plain community, which has a unique way of interacting with the healthcare system. The affected population includes unvaccinated adults and infants.
analysis.event: An ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has resulted in five deaths and a sixth under review, with about 1,300 total reported cases. The death rate is significantly higher than historical averages, and the outbreak is described as the largest and deadliest in the US in over 30 years.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has led to a death rate at least 1.5 times higher than average, with severe outcomes like hospitalizations and deaths being more common. The unique vulnerabilities of the Pennsylvania community, including a high proportion of unvaccinated adults and infants, contribute to the increased risk.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC has sent a disease detective to Pennsylvania to better understand the outbreak's scale and trajectory. However, the data is considered outdated, and underreporting is expected, making it difficult to estimate the true extent of the outbreak. Public health experts are working to refine their understanding of the situation.

analysis.brief_en: An ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has become the largest and deadliest in the US in over 30 years, with five deaths and a sixth under review among about 1,300 cases. The death rate is at least 1.5 times higher than historical averages, and experts suggest this is due to the unique vulnerabilities of the affected community, particularly the Amish and Plain groups, which have a high proportion of unvaccinated adults and infants. The CDC has sent a disease detective to help assess the outbreak's scale and trajectory, but the data remains outdated, and underreporting is expected. Public health officials are concerned about the impact of the outbreak, especially on pregnant women and their babies, as measles complications are more severe for unvaccinated adults. The outbreak highlights the challenges of tracking and responding to measles in a country where it was previously eliminated, and the political tensions over measles deaths complicate efforts to understand the full scope of the situation.

news.title: Measles Update: October 23, 2026
news.excerpt: Today, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported there were 4588* cases of measles in the US as of October 22, 2026. Week-over-week, the agency added 178 cases, a 4.0% increase.

Pylori Norovirus Healthcare Associated Infections (HAI) Prevention Antibiotics Immunizations Vaccines Respiratory Infections Community-Acquired Pneumonia Measles Influenza Sexually Transmitted Diseases HIV / AIDS HPV HSV PrEP Skin & Soft Tissue Diseases MRSA Zoonotic & Vector-Borne Diseases Lyme Disease ZIKA Choose Topic Spotlight - Vaccines in America| Antibiotics Deconstructed| Bench to Bedside With SIDP| Antimicrobial Stewardship| Hepatitis Advertisement News|Articles|October 23, 2026 Measles Update: October 23, 2026 Author(s)Matt Hoffman The latest CDC numbers show a 4.0% increase in measles cases from week-to-week, bringing the 2026 US total to 4588 confirmed cases. Ninety-six percent of cases are outbreak-associated. Advertisement Today, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported there were 4588* cases of measles in the US as of October 22, 2026. Week-over-week, the agency added 178 cases, a 4.0% increase. Last week, the federal agency reported there were 4410* confirmed cases.1,2 The increase is smaller than last week's 8.1% rise, when CDC added 330 cases.2 The 2026 total is now roughly double the 2289 cases reported for all of 2025.1 CDC said there were 4570 measles cases reported by 47 jurisdictions: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York City, New York State, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. A total of 18 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States.1 The federal agency reports there have been 43 new outbreaks** reported in 2026, and 96% of confirmed cases (4404 of 4588) are outbreak-associated (3020 from outbreaks starting in 2026 and 1384 from outbreaks starting in 2025).1 One new outbreak was added since last week.2 Hospitalizations and Age Distribution in 2026 Measles Cases CDC reported 479 hospitalizations among the 4588 cases, or 10%.1 Last week, the agency reported 451 hospitalizations, which means 28 more patients were hospitalized week-over-week.2 Hospitalization rates varied by age. Children younger than 5 years had a rate of 16% (119 of 766), and adults 20 years and older had a rate of 14% (268 of 1881).1 Those aged 5 to 19 years had a rate of 5% (91 of 1914).1 People younger than 20 years account for 58% of cases (2680 of 4588).1 Adults 20 years and older make up 41% (1881 cases), and the age of 27 cases is unknown.1 Vaccination Status and Coverage Trends Ninety-six percent of 2026 patients were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, while 2% had received 1 MMR dose and 2% had received 2 doses.1 CDC lists 3 measles deaths in 2026, a number the agency says is subject to change as reviews are completed.1 Frequently Asked Questions What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious viral disease caused by the measles virus, transmitted through respiratory droplets and airborne particles. It was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 but has resurged due to declining vaccination rates. What are the symptoms of measles? Symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a characteristic red rash spreading from the face downward, typically appearing 3 to 5 days after fever onset. How is measles prevented? The MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine is highly effective, with 2 doses providing approximately 97% protection. The CDC recommends children receive the first dose at 12 to 15 months and the second at 4 to 6 years. Kindergarten MMR coverage has fallen from 95.2% in the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025-2026, leaving approximately 280,000 kindergartners at risk.1 CDC is also working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized case definition for measles deaths.1 *It is important to note that the CDC says on its website that the federal agency is aware of probable measles cases being reported by jurisdictions. However, the data on this page only include confirmed cases that jurisdictions notified the CDC about. Therefore, there could be higher numbers in the US overall. **CDC reports the cumulative number of measles outbreaks (defined as 3 or more related cases) that have occurred this year in the US; states have the most up-to-date information about cases and outbreaks in their jurisdictions. analysis.location_and_population: The measles cases are reported across 47 jurisdictions in the United States, including states like Pennsylvania. analysis.event: The CDC reported a 4.0% week-over-week increase in measles cases, bringing the 2026 US total to 4588 confirmed cases. This is an update on the ongoing measles outbreak in the US, with 3 measles deaths reported in 2026.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: There were 4588 confirmed measles cases in the US as of October 22, 2026, with 96% of cases being outbreak-associated. The CDC reported 479 hospitalizations, or 10% of cases, with higher rates among children under 5 (16%) and adults 20 years and older (14%). The 2026 total is roughly double the 2025 total of 2289 cases. Additionally, 18 measles cases were reported among international visitors.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC is actively monitoring and reporting on measles cases and outbreaks, with a focus on developing a standardized case definition for measles deaths. The data includes only confirmed cases, and the CDC acknowledges that probable cases may exist but are not included in the current statistics.

analysis.brief_en: The article, published on October 23, 2026, reports that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has documented a 4.0% week-over-week increase in measles cases, bringing the 2026 US total to 4588 confirmed cases. This marks a significant rise compared to the 2025 total of 2289 cases, with the 2026 figure being roughly double. Ninety-six percent of these cases are outbreak-associated, and 479 hospitalizations were reported, representing 10% of all cases. The CDC notes that 96% of patients were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, highlighting a decline in immunization rates. The agency is also working on standardizing the case definition for measles deaths. While the article mentions a sixth measles-related death in Pennsylvania, it emphasizes that the data only includes confirmed cases, and probable cases may exist. The CDC continues to monitor the outbreak and is collaborating with state epidemiologists to track the spread and impact of the virus.

The state is the source of about a quarter of this year's measles cases in the U.S. (AP Photo/Matt Rourke) 1 / 4 Trending 1 Illinois man arrested for $665K scam of Escanaba man 2 MMR opens doors 3 Teen pleads no contest in drowning death 4 BraveBots fate uncertain 5 Three measles cases in Delta — first since 1989 6 Registry changes bring Halloween safety into focus 7 Mike in Gladstone view more DELTA COUNTY -- Three cases of measles have been confirmed in Delta County, announced Public Health of Delta & Menominee Counties (PHDM) on Wednesday afternoon. “The health department is working with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) to investigate the cases and notify anyone who may be exposed,” said PHDM in the release. The last time measles appeared in the two-county jurisdiction was 1989. These are the first cases in the Upper Peninsula in 2026. The highly-contagious airborne disease’s common symptoms are high fever, rash, cough and red eyes. The severity and danger, however, is more extreme than most other illnesses; one out of five people who catch it end up hospitalized, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Complications range from effects as mild as an ear infection to as serious as blindness, encephalitis or death. “(Measles) can make you severely ill and lead to life-threatening complications like brain inflammation and pneumonia. It can also make you more likely to get sick with other infections,” says Cleveland Clinic. Before a vaccine was developed in 1963, almost every child in the United States contracted measles before the age of 15. An annual four million cases led to about 500 deaths and 48,000 hospitalizations every year in the U.S., reports the Infectious Diseases Society of America. The measles vaccine was combined with the vaccines for mumps and rubella in 1971; since then, infections fell dramatically, and a two-dose series became common practice. The CDC declared measles eliminated from the United States in 2000 thanks to high coverage with the MMR shots. However, with a noted drop in immunizations since 2019, the disease has been showing up more and more, with a massive surge this year. Ten years ago, the U.S. recorded just 70 confirmed cases of measles in 2016. The country counted 285 in 2024, and then a whopping 2,289 in 2025. In 2026, there have been over 4,000 measles cases. One case can generate up to 18 secondary infections where immunity is low, estimates the World Health Organization. “Measles is highly contagious, which means it spreads easily from person to person. Experts estimate that if one person in a room of unvaccinated people has measles, 9 out of 10 people in the room will catch it,” wrote Cleveland Clinic. “You're contagious about four days before you develop a rash until about four days after the rash starts.” The largest outbreaks in 2026 have been in Pennsylvania, where over 1,300 cases have been confirmed. The State of Pennsylvania states that five individuals have died from measles this year. At the federal level, however, officially only three deaths of 2026 are yet attributed to measles. As part of a directive from U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the CDC recently updated its policy to require that measles-related deaths be verified by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) based on formal death certificates. Regardless, the fact remains that instances of measles -- known to be both very contagious and potentially deadly -- have been rising. In American residents between the years of 2001 and 2015, 1,789 measles cases were reported. That means the number of cases in one year (over 4,600 in 2026) amount to more that double the total seen over a cumulative 14-year span. About 70 percent of observed cases occur in unvaccinated patients. While symptoms may be treated, measles does not have a cure. However, as prevention is far more likely with immunization than without, medical professionals advise that people who can get the vaccine do. The MMR vaccine is live-attenuated, meaning that it contains weakened versions of the viruses that cause measles, mumps and rubella. For most healthy people, two injections four weeks apart provide about 97% protection. Some people, however, cannot tolerate the vaccine; people who are pregnant and those with weakened immune systems are advised to avoid attenuated viruses. There is another option: babies under 12 months, pregnant people and those with weak immune systems may be able to get a different treatment called immunoglobulin (IG). Primarily, though, those people’s health relies on “herd immunity” -- a term for when a population doesn’t see much sickness because a majority of individuals are protected and not spreading contagions. Getting the MMR shot or IG within 72 hours of exposure may stop a person from getting sick. With the measles virus known to be in the community, PHDM recommends some steps: – Check your vaccination status. “You can ask your doctor or contact the local health department,” says PHDM, but notes that people are likely protected if: (a) they have had at least one MMR vaccine, preferably two; (b) they have a record of immunity to measles, such as documented history of a past measles infection; or (c) were born before 1957. PHDM offers MMR vaccines. To make an appointment or ask questions, call PHDM at (906) 786-4111. Most insurance plans cover the vaccine. People may qualify for free or low-costs shots. Talk to your local health department or healthcare provider. – Watch for symptoms. Measles symptoms are high fever, which can reach over 104 degrees; cough; runny nose; red, watery eyes; tiny white spots in the mouth; a red, raised rash that starts on the face and spreads to the body. Symptoms generally show up one to two weeks after exposure but can take up to three weeks to present. – If you get symptoms, call a healthcare provider. The recommendation is to call before seeking medical help in order to avoid spreading the virus. 2 articles remaining... Starting at $4.00/week.
