The last time measles appeared in the two-county jurisdiction was 1989. These are the first cases in the Upper Peninsula in 2026. The highly-contagious airborne disease’s common symptoms are high fever, rash, cough and red eyes. The severity and danger, however, is more extreme than most other illnesses; one out of five people who catch it end up hospitalized, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Complications range from effects as mild as an ear infection to as serious as blindness, encephalitis or death. “(Measles) can make you severely ill and lead to life-threatening complications like brain inflammation and pneumonia. It can also make you more likely to get sick with other infections,” says Cleveland Clinic. Before a vaccine was developed in 1963, almost every child in the United States contracted measles before the age of 15. An annual four million cases led to about 500 deaths and 48,000 hospitalizations every year in the U.S., reports the Infectious Diseases Society of America. The measles vaccine was combined with the vaccines for mumps and rubella in 1971; since then, infections fell dramatically, and a two-dose series became common practice. The CDC declared measles eliminated from the United States in 2000 thanks to high coverage with the MMR shots. However, with a noted drop in immunizations since 2019, the disease has been showing up more and more, with a massive surge this year. Ten years ago, the U.S. recorded just 70 confirmed cases of measles in 2016. The country counted 285 in 2024, and then a whopping 2,289 in 2025. In 2026, there have been over 4,000 measles cases. One case can generate up to 18 secondary infections where immunity is low, estimates the World Health Organization. “Measles is highly contagious, which means it spreads easily from person to person. Experts estimate that if one person in a room of unvaccinated people has measles, 9 out of 10 people in the room will catch it,” wrote Cleveland Clinic. “You're contagious about four days before you develop a rash until about four days after the rash starts.” The largest outbreaks in 2026 have been in Pennsylvania, where over 1,300 cases have been confirmed. The State of Pennsylvania states that five individuals have died from measles this year. At the federal level, however, officially only three deaths of 2026 are yet attributed to measles. As part of a directive from U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the CDC recently updated its policy to require that measles-related deaths be verified by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) based on formal death certificates. Regardless, the fact remains that instances of measles -- known to be both very contagious and potentially deadly -- have been rising. In American residents between the years of 2001 and 2015, 1,789 measles cases were reported. That means the number of cases in one year (over 4,600 in 2026) amount to more that double the total seen over a cumulative 14-year span. About 70 percent of observed cases occur in unvaccinated patients. While symptoms may be treated, measles does not have a cure. However, as prevention is far more likely with immunization than without, medical professionals advise that people who can get the vaccine do. The MMR vaccine is live-attenuated, meaning that it contains weakened versions of the viruses that cause measles, mumps and rubella. For most healthy people, two injections four weeks apart provide about 97% protection. Some people, however, cannot tolerate the vaccine; people who are pregnant and those with weakened immune systems are advised to avoid attenuated viruses. There is another option: babies under 12 months, pregnant people and those with weak immune systems may be able to get a different treatment called immunoglobulin (IG). Primarily, though, those people’s health relies on “herd immunity” -- a term for when a population doesn’t see much sickness because a majority of individuals are protected and not spreading contagions. Getting the MMR shot or IG within 72 hours of exposure may stop a person from getting sick. With the measles virus known to be in the community, PHDM recommends some steps: – Check your vaccination status. “You can ask your doctor or contact the local health department,” says PHDM, but notes that people are likely protected if: (a) they have had at least one MMR vaccine, preferably two; (b) they have a record of immunity to measles, such as documented history of a past measles infection; or (c) were born before 1957. PHDM offers MMR vaccines. To make an appointment or ask questions, call PHDM at (906) 786-4111. Most insurance plans cover the vaccine. People may qualify for free or low-costs shots. Talk to your local health department or healthcare provider. – Watch for symptoms. Measles symptoms are high fever, which can reach over 104 degrees; cough; runny nose; red, watery eyes; tiny white spots in the mouth; a red, raised rash that starts on the face and spreads to the body. Symptoms generally show up one to two weeks after exposure but can take up to three weeks to present. – If you get symptoms, call a healthcare provider. The recommendation is to call before seeking medical help in order to avoid spreading the virus. 2 articles remaining... Starting at $4.00/week. US measles outbreak is proving particularly deadly. Here’s why Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Two infants who were infected with measles have died in Pennsylvania this year, both too young to receive the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine. Hannah Beier/Reuters An ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has quickly become the largest and deadliest in the United States in more than 30 years. Historical data suggests that 1 to 3 people will die out of every 1,000 unvaccinated people who contract measles. But Pennsylvania has reported five measles-associated deaths — with a sixth under review — out of about 1,300 total reported cases since the start of the outbreak in April. This puts the measles death rate in Pennsylvania at least 1.5 times higher than average — and possibly up to 5 times higher. Ad Feedback It’s not likely that the measles virus has changed. One factor might be the size of the outbreak and a probable undercount of cases: It’s difficult to know how many people have been affected. It may also be the unique vulnerabilities of the Pennsylvania community where measles is raging. “There clearly is a shift — not in the biology but a shift in the epidemiology that we’re seeing here in Pennsylvania,” said Dr. Matthew Ferrari, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics at Penn State University. Experts say the outbreak is even larger than official data suggests, and it’s not clear how big it is. The US successfully eliminated measles decades ago, making it difficult to estimate how bad the current resurgence has gotten. A “disease detective” from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention arrived in Pennsylvania this week to help better understand the true scale of the outbreak and its trajectory, the state health department said. The scientist, with the CDC’s Epi-Aid program, is also tasked with evaluating the impact of local vaccination efforts. Scientists and public health workers typically estimate current disease trends by using patterns from recent years, scaling changes against a few variables like birth rates and vaccination rates. But measles data in the US is quite “outdated,” said Dr. Remy Pasco, a research associate at the University of Colorado Boulder. “It’s not endemic, so we don’t have as much data on it. And because the data has been so scarce, anything we can estimate is with a big grain of salt.” Pasco has worked on an analysis to estimate the scale of last year’s measles outbreak in Texas. Some underreporting of cases is expected, he says, but it’s unlikely that the rate of underreporting would be the same — even when comparing recent outbreaks in different parts of the US. There are some “peculiarities” with the outbreak in Pennsylvania, he said. Hospitalization rates with this outbreak are higher than expected. And the Amish and broader Plain community – so named for their simple way of dressing – has a unique way of interacting with the health care system. Severe outcomes, such as hospitalizations and deaths, are generally the best benchmark for understanding how widespread a measles outbreak is, public health experts say. Not every person who is infected with measles will seek care or testing, but severe cases are more visible in the health care system, and tracking them can help set the ratio to understand the full scale. A uniquely susceptible group One signal that this outbreak is different: A disproportionate share of cases are among adults. About two-thirds of measles cases in Pennsylvania have been among adults, and all but a few were unvaccinated. Nationwide, however, cases skew younger; CDC data shows that more than 60% of cases in the US over the past two years have been among children or teens. The large population of unvaccinated adults in Pennsylvania, particularly among Amish and other members of the Plain community, has created a uniquely risky outbreak situation, Ferrari said. Measles complications tend to be more severe for unvaccinated adults than for unvaccinated children, he said. But the low rates of protection among adults in the community also mean vulnerable infants are more likely to be born without protective maternal antibodies. “We normally think about measles as being a childhood infection,” Ferrari said. “Most people have been exposed to measles or have been vaccinated against measles by the time they reach reproductive age.” That’s true around the world. Countries typically have high vaccination rates or endemic measles spread, which means people are exposed when they’re younger. Much of the affected population in Pennsylvania falls into a uniquely susceptible group: both unvaccinated and going decades without exposure because the US had so few cases for so long. news.content_title: Pennsylvania warns of rise in congenital measles and infection during pregnancy
news.content: Oct. 20, 2026, 5:12 PM UTC By Erika Edwards The Pennsylvania Department of Health issued an alert Monday to doctors about an increase in measles infections in pregnant women, as well as a concerning rise in congenital measles — a disease that’s rarely, if ever, seen in the U.S. The department said that 66 pregnant women in Pennsylvania had been diagnosed with measles since the state’s outbreak began in April. “Getting measles while pregnant increases the risk of miscarriage, early labor, and low birth weight,” a department spokesperson said in an email. It’s unclear how many women have miscarried or delivered babies with congenital measles. The department said that state law prohibits it from releasing details of the outcomes of those pregnancies, and there is no national database that tracks cases. True numbers may also be obscured as the outbreak has largely been limited to Amish families who don’t always seek conventional medical assistance. As of Thursday, there have been 4,410 measles cases in the U.S. this year. In Pennsylvania , there have been 1,286 cases as of Monday. Even before widespread measles vaccination, congenital measles was rare. That’s because most women had already been infected as children. It’s only now emerging as a threat as measles outbreaks are increasing as vaccination rates fall. Last month, the American Academy of Pediatrics added a “frequently asked questions” page about congenital measles to its website in response to ongoing and increasing measles outbreaks. According to the AAP, congenital measles occurs in newborns whose mothers have been infected during the two weeks before birth and who test positive or develop measles symptoms within 10 days of delivery. Anecdotally, doctors have said that at least six babies were born in Pennsylvania with congenital measles. Babies can have a range of symptoms, from a rash and fever to pneumonia, neurological problems and low blood platelets. At least two developed pneumonia and were admitted to an intensive care unit, doctors said. Congenital measles can be deadly. One father in Lancaster County previously told NBC News that his wife was sick with measles in August and went into labor a month early. Their baby died shortly after birth. Congenital measles can also lead to severe brain and immune system issues later in life, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said. Those long-term complications can include a very rare and severe inflammatory brain condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE . It can occur seven to 10 years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal. There is evidence that SSPE may occur earlier in children born with congenital measles. There’s no specific treatment for congenital measles other than supportive care, such as fluids, hydration and supplemental oxygen. The best way to prevent the newborn condition is for women to get vaccinated before getting pregnant, the health department said. Pregnant women who get measles are unable to get the vaccine because the shot contains a weakened but live version of the virus. Unvaccinated pregnant women who are exposed to measles can get a dose of immunoglobulin within six days of that exposure, the health department said, to “provide protection against measles infection or reduce the risk of serious illness among susceptible people.” The vaccine can be given to women after they deliver their babies and is safe for breastfeeding mothers, according to state health officials

analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 宾夕法尼亚州卫生部表示,州法律禁止公布妊娠结果的详细信息,并且没有追踪病例的国家数据库。他们强调了怀孕前注射 疫苗接种 的重要性,并提到可以在接触后六天内给未接种疫苗的孕妇注射免疫球蛋白。该部门还强调,暴发 很大程度上仅限于阿米什家庭,这可能会影响数据的准确性。

Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination program faltered in 2025, has reported 202,000 suspected measles cases — 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed — from the start of the outbreak in mid-March to Oct. 9, the World Health Organization said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year. So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94% of reported deaths among children under 5 years old, the WHO said. Bangladesh’s experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95%, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years, but coverage dropped in 2025. 0 seconds of 13 secondsVolume 90% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard ShortcutsEnabledDisabled Play/PauseSPACE Increase Volume↑ Decrease Volume↓ Seek Forward→ Seek Backward← Captions On/Offc Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreenf Mute/Unmutem Decrease Caption Size- Increase Caption Size+ or = Seek %0-9 Play 0.5x1x1.25x1.5x2x Live 00:00 00:13 00:13 00:13 Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak shows no sign of slowing 00:0000:00 A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows that Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents. “This is a real warning to every country,” said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University. Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations is easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said. “The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died,” he said. Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September that the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article. ‘They came only after I buried my son’ In the northeast region of Sylhet, one of the worst-hit areas in the South Asian country of 178 million people, 2-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to a hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family’s three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated 4-year-old sister survived. His father, Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. “They came only after I buried my son,” he said. Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer countries because of factors such as malnutrition. In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the 9-month-old daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency program lowered the vaccination age to 6 months from 9. “No health worker came to tell us,” her father said. In May, Health Minister Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain said the emergency drive had brought cases in hot spots “almost to zero” and that the outbreak was under control. Yet in September, Bangladesh reported a daily average of 1,198 new cases of measles, which causes a high fever, cough and telltale rash. That was the highest total since May. The Bangladesh outbreak comes as vaccine hesitancy is rising, particularly in wealthier countries, amid skepticism championed by figures such as U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In Bangladesh, access to inoculations and awareness are bigger hurdles, experts said. Until recently, Bangladesh had been a vaccination success story. The WHO and the United Nations children’s agency UNICEF estimated that in 2024 it achieved 96% coverage for the first vaccine dose and 93% for the second, which is given to capture the small percentage of children who don’t develop immunity after one shot. Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but it can be deadlier in poorer countries because of factors such as malnutrition.Syed Mahamudur / NurPhoto via Getty But the same year, protests erupted that ended 15 years of rule by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. In the ensuing political turmoil, health workers went on strike, vaccine orders were delayed and follow-up vaccinations that usually accompany routine programs were disrupted. In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated that first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90%, while second-dose coverage was 86%, several percentage points below the 95% needed for herd immunity. The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025. It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100% of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers. Emergency program missed millions Still, when the measles outbreak erupted, Bangladesh responded swiftly and initially seemed to be winning the battle. An emergency program was followed by an initial slowdown in new cases after almost 20 million children received vaccinations in April and May. The government said it had covered every child in the target age group of 6 months to 5 years. But in reality, the program fell short. That emerged when another routine health intervention in June had a target list with 4 million more children than the measles campaign despite covering the same age group. “There is a gap,” prime ministerial adviser Hyder told Reuters on Sept. 14, as measles cases rose again, blaming vaccine hesitancy by parents or child illnesses for keeping children away. Other challenges have also emerged. Documents detailing meetings in April and August between the government, the WHO and other health partners, reviewed by Reuters and not previously reported, show how efforts to act fast may have led to shortcomings. Minutes from the April 19 meeting outlined how the government opted for just one round of so-called readiness checks before launching its emergency vaccination program due to time constraints, instead of the typical four rounds. Checks cover everything from ensuring fridges are available for keeping vaccines cool to determining how many children should be vaccinated. The single round of checks suggested that most — but not all — districts were ready, according to the minutes. The poorest ‘pay the price’ “When preparedness checks are not done properly, it is often the poorest and hardest-to-reach children who miss out on vaccination and pay the price,” said professor Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and chair of Bangladesh’s National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination. Hyder said the April campaign was launched in four weeks. Yet Tajul Islam Abdul Bari, who led immunization in Bangladesh until 2017, said campaigns usually demand months of planning. By the August meeting, shortcomings in the rollout were identified. Minutes noted the proportion of children with confirmed measles cases who had not been vaccinated was “virtually unchanged between pre-campaign (82%) and post-campaign (85%) ... underscoring persistent coverage gaps.” The WHO did not respond to questions about the April and August meetings. But the deputy WHO representative to Bangladesh, Dr. Rajesh Narwal, said the agency was determined to support the government in its goal of vaccinating every child at risk. “Routine immunization must become more effective and resilient so that these gaps do not develop again,” he said. In Sylhet, where official records show 180 children have died, eight of 16 families Reuters interviewed in September said they had not seen health workers offering vaccinations. At least six families said health workers visited only after a child had died from measles in their community. At the end of September, the government launched a new campaign to target 3.4 million children previously missed. “We will involve people across villages so that no child is left behind,” the health minister told a news conference. Yet reaching every child remains a challenge. UNICEF and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics say as many as 40% of children go unregistered, while government data showed that about a third of health worker posts are unfilled. Health experts are also pushing the government to expand the program to vaccinate children over 5. That age group represents a third of measles cases, the WHO says. A child patient at the Infectious Diseases Hospital in Dhaka in March.Abdul Goni / Drik via Getty In addition, scientists in Bangladesh are studying why immunity is waning faster than expected in babies up to 6 months or so. They are usually still protected by maternal antibodies, experts say. Ensuring prompt medical care is vital, the WHO says, another challenge for Bangladesh as it also fights a dengue epidemic. In September, every ward in Sylhet’s 100-bed Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital, which is treating measles, appeared overwhelmed. On the day Reuters visited, 178 patients were admitted. In Sylhet, where official records show 180 children have died, eight of 16 families Reuters interviewed in September said they had not seen health workers offering vaccinations. At least six families said health workers visited only after a child had died from measles in their community. At the end of September, the government launched a new campaign to target 3.4 million children previously missed. “We will involve people across villages so that no child is left behind,” the health minister told a news conference. Yet reaching every child remains a challenge. UNICEF and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics say as many as 40% of children go unregistered, while government data showed that about a third of health worker posts are unfilled. Health experts are also pushing the government to expand the program to vaccinate children over 5. That age group represents a third of measles cases, the WHO says. A child patient at the Infectious Diseases Hospital in Dhaka in March.Abdul Goni / Drik via Getty In addition, scientists in Bangladesh are studying why immunity is waning faster than expected in babies up to 6 months or so. They are usually still protected by maternal antibodies, experts say. Ensuring prompt medical care is vital, the WHO says, another challenge for Bangladesh as it also fights a dengue epidemic. In September, every ward in Sylhet’s 100-bed Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital, which is treating measles, appeared overwhelmed. On the day Reuters visited, 178 patients were admitted. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, October 18, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Measles Virus Genotype D8 Dominates Malaysia as Repeated Importations Fuel Local Outbreaks by October 18, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Measles Virus Genotype D8 Dominates Malaysia as Repeated Importations Fuel Local Outbreaks Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Measles remains one of the most contagious viral diseases known to medicine, and its persistence in countries with apparently high vaccine coverage continues to puzzle public health authorities. A new molecular surveillance study from Malaysia, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, has now provided the most detailed picture yet of how the measles virus circulated across the country between 2018 and 2024. Drawing on 1,110 viral sequences collected nationwide through routine surveillance and outbreak investigations, researchers from the National Public Health Laboratory and partner institutions within the Ministry of Health Malaysia traced the genetic fingerprint of the virus to determine whether measles was quietly endemic in the country or repeatedly arriving from abroad. Their answer, grounded in phylogenetic evidence, points strongly toward repeated importations followed by local amplification, although the authors caution that uninterrupted low-level domestic transmission cannot be entirely excluded. The study’s central finding is the overwhelming predominance of measles virus genotype D8, which accounted for 94 percent of all detections, representing 1,043 of the 1,110 sequences analysed. Genotype B3, another genotype commonly associated with outbreaks in Africa and South Asia, made up 4 percent of detections, while genotype A, which is vaccine-associated and typically signals detection of the attenuated strain contained in the measles vaccine, accounted for the remaining 2 percent. This genotype distribution is significant because the World Health Organization uses the genetic characteristics of the virus, particularly the nucleotide sequence encoding the carboxyl-terminal 450 nucleotides of the nucleoprotein gene, known as the N450 window, to classify measles virus strains and monitor their global movement. Genotyping within this framework allows epidemiologists to distinguish between viral lineages circulating endemically in a region and those imported from countries where measles remains endemic. Discover more Learn Tagalog Read Travel Guides Vaccine To assess temporal trends, the researchers applied logistic regression to the genotype data and found that the odds of detecting genotype D8 increased nearly fourfold per year across the study period, a statistically robust association with a p-value below 0.0001. This steep rise in D8 representation suggests that the lineage became progressively entrenched in the national viral landscape over the seven-year window. Chi-squared tests were used to compare genotype distributions across time and geography, providing a quantitative backbone for the phylogenetic analyses that followed. The combination of classical statistical inference with modern phylogenetic tooling reflects a methodological approach increasingly standard in viral genomic epidemiology, where the goal is not merely to count cases but to reconstruct the transmission history of a pathogen from its genetic sequence data. Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology Order DNA Kits Buy Maps Phylogenetic analyses were performed using the Nextstrain Augur pipeline, an open-source bioinformatics framework widely adopted for real-time pathogen genomic surveillance. The researchers contextualised their Malaysian sequences alongside 28 World Health Organization reference strains, enabling them to place local viral diversity within the global phylogenetic tree of measles virus. The analyses revealed that Malaysian genotype D8 sequences formed a highly conserved lineage, with nucleotide identity ranging from 99.2 to 99.9 percent across the sampled viruses. Molecular clock analyses, which estimate the timing of viral divergence based on the accumulation of mutations over time, further supported the interpretation that multiple phylogenetically distinct clusters appeared across the study period. The presence of these separate clusters, rather than a single continuously evolving lineage, is the key molecular signature that the authors cite as evidence compatible with repeated introductions of the virus from external sources, each followed by local amplification within susceptible populations. Within the sequenced dataset, genotype D8 was first detected in the state of Terengganu in 2018, on the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia. Over the subsequent years, the lineage expanded its geographic footprint, with increased representation in Sabah during 2023 and 2024. Phylogeographic patterns, which combine genetic relatedness with geographic metadata to reconstruct viral movement, were compatible with inter-regional spread involving both Sabah and Peninsular Malaysia. This finding is epidemiologically important because Sabah, one of Malaysia’s two states on the island of Borneo, has historically faced challenges in vaccination delivery due to geographic remoteness, undocumented migration, and variable healthcare access. The genetic evidence of viral movement between Sabah and the peninsula underscores the interconnectedness of Malaysia’s measles epidemiology across its two landmasses separated by the South China Sea. Discover more Find Vaccines vaccine public health The demographic profile of measles cases in the study reveals a critical vulnerability in Malaysia’s immunisation landscape. Most cases occurred among unvaccinated children and adolescents, indicating that the primary driver of measles transmission is the presence of individuals who have not received the recommended doses of measles-containing vaccine. However, a notable 29 percent of sequenced cases occurred in previously vaccinated individuals, a proportion that warrants careful interpretation. Vaccine failure can arise from primary vaccine failure, where an individual fails to develop an adequate immune response after vaccination, or secondary vaccine failure, where immunity wanes over time. Alternatively, some vaccinated cases may reflect incorrect vaccination records or incomplete dose history. The relatively high proportion of breakthrough cases, if confirmed through serological assessment, could suggest gaps in population-level immunity that extend beyond the unvaccinated population. Malaysia has reported high measles vaccine coverage through its National Immunisation Programme, which provides two doses of measles-containing vaccine to children at nine months and twelve months of age. The persistence of measles despite this coverage highlights the concept of immunity gaps, where pockets of susceptible individuals, whether due to vaccine hesitancy, access barriers, migration, or waning immunity, create conditions sufficient for viral amplification when the virus is introduced. The WHO framework for measles elimination requires that a country demonstrate the absence of endemic measles virus transmission for at least 36 consecutive months, with all cases confirmed as importation-related through molecular surveillance. The Malaysian study’s finding that molecular patterns are compatible with repeated introductions rather than endemic persistence is therefore encouraging from an elimination standpoint, as it suggests that the country may be closer to interrupting transmission than case numbers alone would indicate. The distinction between endemic persistence and repeated importation is not merely academic. It has direct implications for public health strategy. If measles were endemic, the priority would be to strengthen routine immunisation and conduct supplementary immunisation activities to close immunity gaps. If measles is primarily imported, the emphasis shifts toward border health measures, rapid outbreak response, contact tracing, and targeted catch-up vaccination in communities with identified susceptibility. The Malaysian study’s phylogenetic evidence, showing multiple distinct clusters appearing and disappearing over time rather than a single continuously evolving lineage, supports the latter interpretation. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation that low-level domestic transmission, occurring below the detection threshold of the surveillance system, cannot be definitively ruled out without more intensive sampling and sequencing. The study also contributes to the broader regional picture of measles epidemiology in Southeast Asia, where several countries have experienced measles resurgence in recent years following disruptions to immunisation services during the COVID-19 pandemic. The WHO South-East Asia and Western Pacific regions have set elimination goals, and molecular surveillance is a cornerstone of the verification process. The Malaysian dataset, spanning seven years and over a thousand sequences, represents one of the larger national measles sequence collections in the region and provides a valuable reference for neighbouring countries conducting their own phylogenetic analyses. The researchers acknowledge the WHO Measles Nucleotide Surveillance database, known as MeaNS, for providing the reference sequences used to contextualise their findings within the global measles virus phylogeny. Looking forward, the study’s findings suggest several priorities for strengthening measles control in Malaysia. Closing immunity gaps among unvaccinated children and adolescents remains the most direct intervention, and the identification of specific states and age groups where susceptibility is concentrated provides actionable targets for immunisation campaigns. The phylogeographic evidence of inter-regional spread between Sabah and Peninsular Malaysia highlights the need for coordinated surveillance and response across both landmasses. Continued investment in molecular surveillance, including routine sequencing of measles virus detections and integration of phylogenetic analyses into national outbreak investigations, will be essential for verifying elimination status and responding rapidly to future importations. The research received no specific external funding and was conducted using anonymised surveillance data from the National Public Health Laboratory, with ethical approval from the Medical Research and Ethics Committee of the Ministry of Health Malaysia. However, a notable 29 percent of sequenced cases occurred in previously vaccinated individuals, a proportion that warrants careful interpretation. Vaccine failure can arise from primary vaccine failure, where an individual fails to develop an adequate immune response after vaccination, or secondary vaccine failure, where immunity wanes over time. Alternatively, some vaccinated cases may reflect incorrect vaccination records or incomplete dose history. The relatively high proportion of breakthrough cases, if confirmed through serological assessment, could suggest gaps in population-level immunity that extend beyond the unvaccinated population. Malaysia has reported high measles vaccine coverage through its National Immunisation Programme, which provides two doses of measles-containing vaccine to children at nine months and twelve months of age. The persistence of measles despite this coverage highlights the concept of immunity gaps, where pockets of susceptible individuals, whether due to vaccine hesitancy, access barriers, migration, or waning immunity, create conditions sufficient for viral amplification when the virus is introduced. The WHO framework for measles elimination requires that a country demonstrate the absence of endemic measles virus transmission for at least 36 consecutive months, with all cases confirmed as importation-related through molecular surveillance. The Malaysian study’s finding that molecular patterns are compatible with repeated introductions rather than endemic persistence is therefore encouraging from an elimination standpoint, as it suggests that the country may be closer to interrupting transmission than case numbers alone would indicate. The distinction between endemic persistence and repeated importation is not merely academic. It has direct implications for public health strategy. If measles were endemic, the priority would be to strengthen routine immunisation and conduct supplementary immunisation activities to close immunity gaps. If measles is primarily imported, the emphasis shifts toward border health measures, rapid outbreak response, contact tracing, and targeted catch-up vaccination in communities with identified susceptibility. The Malaysian study’s phylogenetic evidence, showing multiple distinct clusters appearing and disappearing over time rather than a single continuously evolving lineage, supports the latter interpretation. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation that low-level domestic transmission, occurring below the detection threshold of the surveillance system, cannot be definitively ruled out without more intensive sampling and sequencing. The study also contributes to the broader regional picture of measles epidemiology in Southeast Asia, where several countries have experienced measles resurgence in recent years following disruptions to immunisation services during the COVID-19 pandemic. The WHO South-East Asia and Western Pacific regions have set elimination goals, and molecular surveillance is a cornerstone of the verification process. The Malaysian dataset, spanning seven years and over a thousand sequences, represents one of the larger national measles sequence collections in the region and provides a valuable reference for neighbouring countries conducting their own phylogenetic analyses. The researchers acknowledge the WHO Measles Nucleotide Surveillance database, known as MeaNS, for providing the reference sequences used to contextualise their findings within the global measles virus phylogeny. Looking forward, the study’s findings suggest several priorities for strengthening measles control in Malaysia. Closing immunity gaps among unvaccinated children and adolescents remains the most direct intervention, and the identification of specific states and age groups where susceptibility is concentrated provides actionable targets for immunisation campaigns. The phylogeographic evidence of inter-regional spread between Sabah and Peninsular Malaysia highlights the need for coordinated surveillance and response across both landmasses. Continued investment in molecular surveillance, including routine sequencing of measles virus detections and integration of phylogenetic analyses into national outbreak investigations, will be essential for verifying elimination status and responding rapidly to future importations. The research received no specific external funding and was conducted using anonymised surveillance data from the National Public Health Laboratory, with ethical approval from the Medical Research and Ethics Committee of the Ministry of Health Malaysia. The authors caution that low-level domestic transmission cannot be definitively ruled out without more intensive sampling. The study underscores the importance of addressing vaccine hesitancy, access barriers, and waning immunity to prevent further outbreaks.

news.content: News Health Pennsylvania issues clinical alert over congenital measles — Ars Technica Fedir Kryshtovskyi 20 October 2026 02:52 The Pennsylvania Department of Health in the United States has issued a clinical alert for medical professionals due to a rise in measles cases during pregnancy and related cases of congenital measles in newborns. Before the current outbreak, such cases had not been recorded in the United States for decades, Ars Technica reports . Scale of the outbreak As of October 19, Pennsylvania had recorded 1,286 measles cases in 42 counties since the beginning of the year. Of these, 247 people were hospitalized. Six deaths were reported during the outbreak, although the latest of these cases is still being reviewed by the state health department before being added to official statistics. In early October, The 19th reported 53 cases of measles during pregnancy. At least one case of congenital measles resulted in death: a newborn boy died immediately after birth while his mother was severely ill with measles. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Risks for pregnant women and infants Measles during pregnancy increases the risk of hospitalization, pneumonia, the need for oxygen support or mechanical ventilation, and death. The infection is also associated with a higher risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, and premature birth. The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy because it is a live attenuated vaccine. Pregnant women without measles vaccination or a previous infection who have been exposed to the virus are advised to receive intravenous immunoglobulin within six days of exposure. The virus can be transmitted to the fetus in utero or infect a child during or immediately after delivery. In infants, congenital measles may manifest as fever, jaundice, rash, low platelet levels, pneumonia, and neurological complications. Children who survive the acute infection require long-term monitoring due to the risk of immune amnesia and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a progressive fatal neurological disease that can occur years after infection. news.content_original: News Health Pennsylvania issues clinical alert over congenital measles — Ars Technica Fedir Kryshtovskyi 20 October 2026 02:52 The Pennsylvania Department of Health in the United States has issued a clinical alert for medical professionals due to a rise in measles cases during pregnancy and related cases of congenital measles in newborns. Before the current outbreak, such cases had not been recorded in the United States for decades, Ars Technica reports . Scale of the outbreak As of October 19, Pennsylvania had recorded 1,286 measles cases in 42 counties since the beginning of the year. Of these, 247 people were hospitalized. Six deaths were reported during the outbreak, although the latest of these cases is still being reviewed by the state health department before being added to official statistics. In early October, The 19th reported 53 cases of measles during pregnancy. At least one case of congenital measles resulted in death: a newborn boy died immediately after birth while his mother was severely ill with measles. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Risks for pregnant women and infants Measles during pregnancy increases the risk of hospitalization, pneumonia, the need for oxygen support or mechanical ventilation, and death. The infection is also associated with a higher risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, and premature birth. The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy because it is a live attenuated vaccine. Pregnant women without measles vaccination or a previous infection who have been exposed to the virus are advised to receive intravenous immunoglobulin within six days of exposure. The virus can be transmitted to the fetus in utero or infect a child during or immediately after delivery. In infants, congenital measles may manifest as fever, jaundice, rash, low platelet levels, pneumonia, and neurological complications. Children who survive the acute infection require long-term monitoring due to the risk of immune amnesia and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a progressive fatal neurological disease that can occur years after infection. news.content: Türkiye Economy Opinion World Arts & Life Sports Photo Measles cases surge past 3,000 in Türkiye as vaccination coverage falls News Türkiye October 20 2026 09:46:40 Measles cases surge past 3,000 in Türkiye as vaccination coverage falls Selin Irmak Kaçmaz - ISTANBUL Two vaccine doses provide approximately 97-99 percent protection against measles, experts say. Measles cases in Türkiye have surged to nearly 3,000 in October 2026, raising concerns over declining vaccination rates and the risk of further outbreaks, according to figures cited by the Turkish Medical Association and infectious disease specialists. Advertisement Next Stay Close ✕ Ad loading Haberin Devamı The highly contagious virus can infect 16 to 18 people through a single patient, making it one of the most transmissible infectious diseases. Cases in Türkiye rose from 127 in 2022 to 500 in 2023, 1,500 in 2024 and around 2,000 in 2025, according to World Health Organization data. Experts say falling vaccination coverage, vaccine hesitancy and gaps in immunization tracking are contributing to the resurgence. Measles vaccination coverage in Türkiye has reportedly fallen to around 92 percent, below the 95 percent threshold considered necessary to prevent sustained transmission. The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is administered free of charge through Türkiye’s national immunization program, with doses scheduled at 12 months and again at age four to six. Two doses provide protection to approximately 97-99 percent of recipients, experts say. Infectious disease specialist Songül Özer warned that the disease is increasingly affecting adults as well as children and can cause serious complications. Around 30 percent of reported cases develop at least one complication such as pneumonia, encephalitis (inflammation of the brain) and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), according to experts. news.content: 24/7 LiveSan FranciscoEast BaySouth BayPeninsulaNorth Bay 67° Measles US surpasses 1,000 measles cases for the 3rd time in 26 years, CDC data shows Cases have been confirmed in 27 states, CDC data shows. Watch ABC News live news stream and get 24/7 latest, breaking news coverage, and live video. ByMary Kekatos Friday, February 27, 2026 Share Measles cases have topped 1,000 in the United States for the third time in 26 years. At least 154 new measles cases have been confirmed in the last week for a total of 1,136, according to updated data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). So far this year, cases have been confirmed in 27 states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin. Just six measles cases were reported among international travelers so far this year, according to CDC data. About 92% of cases are among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, CDC data shows. Meanwhile, 4% of cases are among those who have received just one dose of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine and 4% of cases are among those who received the recommended two doses, according to the CDC. The current measles situation in the U.S. is partly being driven by a large outbreak in South Carolina that began last year, with 979 cases recorded as of Friday, according to state health officials. Top Stories El Niño: SF declares local emergency to prepare for potential severe storms, coastal flooding $300K reward offered in 1987 Daly City cold case murder of Michelle Matteucci 1 minute ago 2 killed in 5-car crash on I-280 in Los Altos after driver crossed into oncoming traffic: CHP Last year, the U.S. recorded 2,281 measles cases, which is the highest number of national cases in 33 years, according to the CDC. Before that, the last time measles cases rose above 1,000 was 2019 -- CDC data showed 1,274 that year. Recorded cases dropped to a low of 13 in 2020, the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic. It also marked the first U.S. deaths recorded from measles in a decade, two among school-aged unvaccinated children in Texas and a third of an unvaccinated adult in New Mexico. The CDC currently recommends people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective, and two doses are 97% effective against measles, according to the CDC. However, federal data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2024-2025 school year, 92.5% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 92.7% seen in the previous school year and the 95.2% seen in the 2019-2020 school year, before the COVID-19 pandemic. So far this year, cases have been confirmed in 27 states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin. Just six measles cases were reported among international travelers so far this year, according to CDC data. About 92% of cases are among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, CDC data shows. Meanwhile, 4% of cases are among those who have received just one dose of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine and 4% of cases are among those who received the recommended two doses, according to the CDC. The current measles situation in the U.S. is partly being driven by a large outbreak in South Carolina that began last year, with 979 cases recorded as of Friday, according to state health officials. Before that, the last time measles cases rose above 1,000 was 2019 -- CDC data showed 1,274 that year. Recorded cases dropped to a low of 13 in 2020, the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic. It also marked the first U.S. deaths recorded from measles in a decade, two among school-aged unvaccinated children in Texas and a third of an unvaccinated adult in New Mexico. The CDC currently recommends people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective, and two doses are 97% effective against measles, according to the CDC. However, federal data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2024-2025 school year, 92.5% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 92.7% seen in the previous school year and the 95.2% seen in the 2019-2020 school year, before the COVID-19 pandemic. news.content_title: DuPage County measles case prompts exposure alert at Chicago's O'Hare airport
news.content: 24/7 LiveChicago & Suburban Cook Co.North SuburbsWest SuburbsSouth SuburbsNW Indiana 63° Measles DuPage County measles case prompts exposure alert at Chicago's O'Hare airport A DuPage County measles case has prompted an exposure alert at Chicago O'Hare International Airport, health officials said. ByCate Cauguiran Friday, October 23, 2026 3:31AM Share CHICAGO (WLS) -- Chicago and DuPage County health officials are urging people who may have been exposed to measles to watch for symptoms after what officials describe as a rare breakthrough case involving a vaccinated DuPage County resident. ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch The first confirmed measles case in DuPage County this year has prompted an exposure alert at O'Hare International Airport. Public health officials say anyone who was in Terminal 5 on Oct. 15 between 4:20 p.m. and 7 p.m. may have been exposed after a DuPage County resident tested positive for measles following international travel. Health officials are encouraging anyone who may have been at the airport during that time to monitor for symptoms and know what steps to take if they become ill. "If you suspect that you have contracted measles or that you've been exposed to measles, call ahead if you're going to go to an emergency room or urgent care. Call ahead so they can establish some isolation protocols," said Dr. Constantine Kanakis, a clinical pathologist at Northwestern Memorial Hospital. According to health officials, symptoms of measles can include fever, rash, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Officials say symptoms may develop up to 21 days after exposure. Top Stories E. coli cases possibly linked to Bengtson's Pumpkin Farm, Will County health officials say 1 hour ago Married couple found dead in car in apparent murder-suicide, Bradley police say 1 hour ago Semi crash closes multiple lanes on I-80 in Will County, Illinois State Police say 2 hours ago RELATED | New map shows how to spot the measles risk level in your ZIP code While officials say the risk to the public remains low, they continue to emphasize the importance of vaccination. "Vaccines offer excellent, but not perfect protection from things like measles and other viruses. And the more people that are vaccinated, the less breakthrough cases happen," Kanakis said. The DuPage County case comes as measles cases continue to rise across the United States. "The data shows that cases are indeed going up. Last year, at the same time, there were 2289 cases last fall. The same calendar time this year in 2026, there are almost double that, 4410 cases per the CDC," Kanakis said. ByCate Cauguiran Friday, October 23, 2026 3:31AM Share CHICAGO (WLS) -- Chicago and DuPage County health officials are urging people who may have been exposed to measles to watch for symptoms after what officials describe as a rare breakthrough case involving a vaccinated DuPage County resident. ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch The first confirmed measles case in DuPage County this year has prompted an exposure alert at O'Hare International Airport. Public health officials say anyone who was in Terminal 5 on Oct. 15 between 4:20 p.m. and 7 p.m. may have been exposed after a DuPage County resident tested positive for measles following international travel. Health officials are encouraging anyone who may have been at the airport during that time to monitor for symptoms and know what steps to take if they become ill. "If you suspect that you have contracted measles or that you've been exposed to measles, call ahead if you're going to go to an emergency room or urgent care. Call ahead so they can establish some isolation protocols," said Dr. Constantine Kanakis, a clinical pathologist at Northwestern Memorial Hospital. According to health officials, symptoms of measles can include fever, rash, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Officials say symptoms may develop up to 21 days after exposure. Top Stories E. coli cases possibly linked to Bengtson's Pumpkin Farm, Will County health officials say 1 hour ago Married couple found dead in car in apparent murder-suicide, Bradley police say 1 hour ago Semi crash closes multiple lanes on I-80 in Will County, Illinois State Police say 2 hours ago RELATED | New map shows how to spot the measles risk level in your ZIP code While officials say the risk to the public remains low, they continue to emphasize the importance of vaccination. "Vaccines offer excellent, but not perfect protection from things like measles and other viruses. And the more people that are vaccinated, the less breakthrough cases happen," Kanakis said. The DuPage County case comes as measles cases continue to rise across the United States. "The data shows that cases are indeed going up. Last year, at the same time, there were 2289 cases last fall. The same calendar time this year in 2026, there are almost double that, 4410 cases per the CDC," Kanakis said. Health officials say anyone who develops symptoms after a potential exposure should contact a healthcare provider before going to a doctor's office, urgent care facility or emergency room to help prevent additional exposures and allow healthcare facilities to take appropriate precautions. news.title: Measles is spreading in Chester County, but many schools aren’t talking about their risk - Inquirer.com
news.rss_summary_html: Measles is spreading in Chester County, but many schools aren’t talking about their risk  Inquirer.com
news.excerpt_original: Measles is spreading in Chester County, but many schools aren’t talking about their risk Inquirer.com

news.content_title: The Philadelphia Inquirer, LLC
news.content: As the nation's worst measles outbreak spreads, the West Chester Area School District is among those facing declining vaccination rates — and challenges in preparing. Lynn April has seen chatter on social media from parents in her community, expressing hesitancy about giving their children vaccines. But she was shocked to hear that numerous elementary schools in the West Chester Area School District had seen crucial immunization rates fall, as a vaccine-preventable measles outbreak expands into Chester County . “I would think the majority of parents I am associated with would also find that pretty horrifying,” said April, who has a third grader and a fifth grader at East Goshen Elementary. The suburban district reflects a trend worrying health experts: Fewer families are choosing to vaccinate their kids. In West Chester, five of the district’s 11 elementary schools reported kindergarten measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination rates last school year below 95% — the threshold long considered necessary to ensure community protection. One school, Penn Wood Elementary, appeared especially high risk, with only 87.5% vaccinated. Three private schools in or on the border of the district also reported concerningly low kindergarten MMR vaccination rates. Yet school leaders in West Chester have not issued community messages highlighting the risk of the current measles outbreak. Nor are they sharing school-by-school vaccination data that indicate risky pockets within a district of about 12,000 students that touts an overall high vaccination rate. West Chester Superintendent David Christopher questioned whether his community remains as exposed as state data collected last school year suggest. District nurses have called families that didn’t have vaccination records on file, Christopher said, and accounting for all grade levels, every school campus has a vaccination rate above 95%. “We’re really talking about a pretty small percentage of students in the district,” Christopher said in an interview. Even small declines in vaccination rates within a grade level, however, can increase community risk, health experts said. With the nation’s largest measles outbreak in decades spreading across the state, René Najera, director of public health at the College of Physicians of Philadelphia, says a high vaccination rate no longer creates a comfort zone. “It’s some comfort, but it’s not enough, especially in an epidemic situation,” Najera said. “You could have a population with 96% vaccinated, and still have a roaring infection go through.” Christopher said he’s aware the ongoing measles outbreak could bring significant disruption: Earlier this month, a reported measles case led Oxford Area High School to shut down for a day to verify vaccination records for staff members. “The nature of it — you could have one student in a building, and the entire building exposed — is concerning,” Christopher said. Across the Philadelphia region, vaccination rates have been dropping, with at least 40% of area schools reporting kindergarten measles vaccination rates in 2025 below the threshold for what scientists call “herd immunity.” Kindergarten vaccination rates are considered a bellwether for a community’s attitudes toward vaccination, as parents are deciding whether to get the shots required by law to attend school. And increasingly, families are refusing vaccines . Pennsylvania has some of the loosest vaccine exemption policies in the nation, broadly allowing families to pass on immunizations required for school entry by claiming religious, philosophical, or medical objections. At West Chester’s Penn Wood Elementary, MMR vaccination rates among kindergartners fell 8 percentage points last year, with 56 out of 64 kindergartners vaccinated. Five students had philosophical exemptions to the vaccine, according to state data. (Another four were “noncompliant but attending,” a term the state uses for children who haven’t submitted exemption records but are in school.) At Westtown-Thornbury, MMR vaccinations dropped from 100% of kindergartners two years ago to under 92% last year — seemingly because of seven students claiming religious exemptions to vaccination. Sue Gramling, the president of Westtown-Thornbury’s parent-teacher organization, declined to comment about the school’s rate, saying in a message that she didn’t want to speak on behalf of the PTO “since this is such a hot topic right now.” Two other West Chester elementaries with kindergarten MMR rates below the 95% threshold, Glen Acres and East Goshen, also recorded declines in the past year. Christopher said those rates are dated. Nurses later called families who hadn’t submitted vaccination paperwork, more provided records, and some additional students have been vaccinated, he said. Asked whether nurses had called families who opted out through legal exemptions, Christopher said in an email that “the connections have been to ensure that families are educated to make informed decisions about vaccines.” “We understand that there are a variety of reasons that families may make this decision, and it is not our intention to pressure families, but to make sure they are informed,” he said. As community organizations, schools have a responsibility to help disseminate information that affects their students and staff, said Holley Wilkin, an associate professor of communications at Georgia State University who specializes in health communication. “With something like measles, it’s affecting their students and they should be playing that role,” she said. To help communities understand their risk, Pennsylvania’s health department published school-level vaccination data this summer for the first time. » READ MORE: More Philly-area classrooms are seeing lower measles vaccination rates. How protected is your school? Public health officials have warned since the summer that measles is actively circulating along Chester County’s western border with Lancaster County, the center of the state’s current outbreak. But schools appear reluctant to talk about measles planning. Of 12 Chester County school districts contacted by The Inquirer about their preparations, only West Chester agreed to an interview. news.content_original: As the nation's worst measles outbreak spreads, the West Chester Area School District is among those facing declining vaccination rates — and challenges in preparing. Lynn April has seen chatter on social media from parents in her community, expressing hesitancy about giving their children vaccines. But she was shocked to hear that numerous elementary schools in the West Chester Area School District had seen crucial immunization rates fall, as a vaccine-preventable measles outbreak expands into Chester County . “I would think the majority of parents I am associated with would also find that pretty horrifying,” said April, who has a third grader and a fifth grader at East Goshen Elementary. The suburban district reflects a trend worrying health experts: Fewer families are choosing to vaccinate their kids. In West Chester, five of the district’s 11 elementary schools reported kindergarten measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination rates last school year below 95% — the threshold long considered necessary to ensure community protection. Three private schools in or on the border of the district also reported concerningly low kindergarten MMR vaccination rates. OffOn Stream on New York declares state disaster emergency over rising measles cases. Here's what that means New York has recorded 108 measles cases so far this year, most since mid-July. ByMary Kekatos and Dr. Jade Cobern October 6, 2026, 6:57 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency on Monday as neighboring Pennsylvania battles its largest measles outbreak in three decades. As of Oct. 3, New York has recorded 108 measles cases so far this year, 92 of those since mid-July across 18 rural counties where communities are under-immunized, according to Hochul's order. "After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a state disaster emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease," Hochul said in a statement. "No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease." Related Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania amid the state's largest outbreak in decades It marks the first time a state has issued an emergency order since measles cases began rising last year. At least 95% of measles cases in the U.S. have been among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown. The order allows registered nurses to order the collection and testing of specimens for suspected measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul speaks during a news conference, Oct. 2, 2026, in New York. Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo Early symptoms include cough, runny nose, fever as high as 104 Fahrenheit and red, watery eyes, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Two to three days after symptoms start, patients may develop Koplik spots, which are tiny white spots that may appear inside the mouth on the inner cheek. Three to five days after symptoms start, patients may experience a rash, first appearing on the face at the hairline before moving downwards to the neck, chest, stomach, arms, legs and feet. Fever may spike even higher than 104 F when the rash appears, the CDC says. The order, in effect until Nov. 4, allows pharmacists in New York to vaccinate children as young as age 2 with the MMR shot. It also expands who can administer MMR vaccines to include emergency medical technicians-paramedics, advanced EMS and midwives. Additionally, it suspends a previous requirement that health care professionals who administer vaccines to those aged 19 and older receive consent before reporting vaccination to New York City or New York State immunizations registries. All MMR vaccinations of children and adults must be reported within 72 hours. Related How hospitals, clinics in Pennsylvania are responding to the measles outbreak "Department staff are working closely with local health departments and regional partners to track and contain the current measles outbreak," Dr. James McDonald, commissioner for the New York State Department, said in a statement. "The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is the best protection -- protecting nearly all people against disease who receive the recommended doses." Popular Reads Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Oct 16 France reports 1st known human case of Shamonda virus 1 day ago Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress 2 days ago The state said it has administered more than 1,000 MMR shots in rural areas since July. Meanwhile, Pennsylvania health officials are now reporting more than 1,000 measles cases. Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and the state has reported five measles-associated deaths, which is the most any state has reported in over 30 years. This outbreak follows a trend of growing outbreaks in the U.S. over the last two years. Earlier this year, South Carolina reported the end to a measles outbreak of 997 cases. Last year, Texas reported an outbreak of 762 cases. Measles virus particle, illustration. Kateryna Kon/science Photo Library/Getty Images Nationally, nearly 4,000 cases have been confirmed this year in the U.S., with infections reported in almost every state, according to the CDC. It's the highest number of illnesses from measles since 1991. The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection, and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says. Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine. However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025-26 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019-20 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. School vaccine exemptions also reached a record high last school year. Recent CDC data showed that vaccine exemptions for kindergarteners increased to 4.2% during the 2025-26 school year. This is up from 3.6% compared to the previous school year and 2.2% during the 2020-21 school year. analysis.time: New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared the state disaster emergency on Monday, October 6, 2026, and the order is in effect until November 4, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: New York State, specifically 18 rural counties where communities are under-immunized, and the U.S. as a whole, with measles cases reported in almost every state.
analysis.event: New York declared a state disaster emergency due to a rising number of measles cases, which are primarily among unvaccinated individuals. The declaration was made by Governor Kathy Hochul following a review of the latest data on measles cases.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: New York has recorded 108 measles cases this year, with 92 since mid-July. Nationally, nearly 4,000 cases have been confirmed this year, the highest since 1991. In Pennsylvania, over 1,000 measles cases have been reported, with 200 hospitalizations and five deaths. The CDC recommends two doses of the MMR vaccine for protection, with one dose being 93% effective and two doses 97% effective.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The state has implemented measures to expand MMR vaccine administration, allowing pharmacists and emergency medical technicians to vaccinate children as young as age 2. The order also suspends a previous requirement for consent when reporting vaccinations for those aged 19 and older. All MMR vaccinations must be reported within 72 hours.

analysis.brief_en: New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency on October 6, 2026, due to a surge in measles cases, with 108 reported this year, 92 since mid-July, primarily in under-immunized rural areas. The emergency order, effective until November 4, 2026, allows pharmacists and emergency medical technicians to administer MMR vaccines to children as young as age 2 and expands vaccine access. It also suspends the requirement for consent when reporting vaccinations for individuals aged 19 and older. Nationally, nearly 4,000 measles cases have been confirmed this year, the highest since 1991, with over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania, resulting in 200 hospitalizations and five deaths. The CDC emphasizes the importance of two MMR doses for protection, with 97% effectiveness, and notes that vaccination rates have declined, contributing to the outbreak. The state has administered over 1,000 MMR shots since July, aiming to increase immunization coverage.

The emergency order, effective until November 4, 2026, allows pharmacists and emergency medical technicians to administer MMR vaccines to children as young as age 2 and expands vaccine access. It also suspends the requirement for consent when reporting vaccinations for individuals aged 19 and older. Nationally, nearly 4,000 measles cases have been confirmed this year, the highest since 1991, with over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania, resulting in 200 hospitalizations and five deaths. The CDC emphasizes the importance of two MMR doses for protection, with 97% effectiveness, and notes that vaccination rates have declined, contributing to the outbreak. The state has administered over 1,000 MMR shots since July, aiming to increase immunization coverage.

news.title_zh: 纽约州因 麻疹 病例不断增加而宣布进入国家灾难紧急状态。这就是它的含义 - ABC 新闻 - 突发新闻、最新新闻和视频
news.source_body_en: New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency on October 6, 2026, due to a surge in measles cases, with 108 reported this year, 92 since mid-July, primarily in under-immunized rural areas. The emergency order, effective until November 4, 2026, allows pharmacists and emergency medical technicians to administer MMR vaccines to children as young as age 2 and expands vaccine access. It also suspends the requirement for consent when reporting vaccinations for individuals aged 19 and older. Nationally, nearly 4,000 measles cases have been confirmed this year, the highest since 1991, with over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania, resulting in 200 hospitalizations and five deaths. The CDC emphasizes the importance of two MMR doses for protection, with 97% effectiveness, and notes that vaccination rates have declined, contributing to the outbreak. The state has administered over 1,000 MMR shots since July, aiming to increase immunization coverage.
news.content_zh: 由于 麻疹 病例激增,纽约州州长 Kathy Hochul 于 2026 年 10 月 6 日宣布进入州灾难紧急状态,今年报告了 108 例,自 7 月中旬以来报告了 92 例,主要发生在免疫不足的农村地区。该紧急命令有效期至 2026 年 11 月 4 日,允许药剂师和紧急医疗技术人员为 2 岁以下的儿童注射 MMR 疫苗,并扩大 疫苗 的使用范围。它还暂停了 19 岁及以上个人报告 疫苗接种 时征得同意的要求。在全国范围内,今年已确诊近 4,000 例 麻疹 病例,为 1991 年以来的最高水平,其中宾夕法尼亚州有 1,000 多例病例,导致 200 人住院治疗,5 人死亡。CDC 强调了两剂 MMR 疫苗对保护的重要性,其有效性为 97%,并指出 疫苗接种 率有所下降,从而促成了 暴发。自 7 月以来,该州已注射了 1,000 多次 MMR 疫苗,旨在提高免疫覆盖率。
